human_text: By professing anti-Platonism, Laas does not want to defend everything that could fall under it, but only what he calls positivism. Positivism is namely: that philosophy which recognizes no other foundations than positive facts, that is, outer and inner perceptions; which demands of every belief that it prove the facts, the experiences, on which the belief rests.Thus “the positivist… is at the same time a sensualist.” Sensualism is an approach for the explanation of phenomenon within our conscious life that begins with the given. In Laas' own words:The sensualist fundamental claim [is that] that all higher mental processes and states, including even thinking, “knowing,” that is, “reason,” are to be grasped as lawfully “transformed” perceptions and lived experiences of feeling, needing, memory-endowed, spontaneously moving beings (animalia), [and for this claim] no more than facts are taken into account. Nowhere does the sensualist reach out to contents and processes that cannot be experienced, that cannot be scientifically constituted. And to no extent does the sensualist claim that they have already succeeded in what they are striving for with their “explanations”; that the sensualist has already truly grasped all supposedly particular differentiations of consciousness as gradual ones: the sensualist thus holds for the time being to the fact which surely does not speak against them, and that up to now both “thinking” and all higher mental functions in the course of time have only ever been encountered as something subsequent, as something behind original perception, behind animalistic desire [animalischem Begehren].In short, Laas fundamentally viewed the possibilities of philosophy differently than the idealists Plato and Kant. The latter had claimed that every person possesses a mental faculty called reason whereas wants to begin epistemology and ethics with solely with what we experience and perceive. According to Laas, historically speaking, Kant had merely replaced the previous scholastic metaphysics with a different term. Sensualists or positivists deny entities such as God and reason, and assert that all thinking, judging, and representations are fundamentally based on “sensory sensations” or “perceptions” or “facts.” For Laas, contrary to all experience, idealists claim that the faculty of “reason” determines thought and action and can judge everything, even what a person has not yet experienced.
ai_text: Laas’ anti-Platonism targets positivism rather than Platonism as a whole, situating his critique within a debate over the foundations of knowledge and justification. Positivism maintains that philosophy rests solely on positive facts—both external perceptions and internal experiences—and demands that any belief be proven by those facts or experiences; in this sense the approach is inherently sensualist, seeking to explain phenomena from within conscious life starting with the given. Laas aligns with a sensualist position by arguing that higher mental processes, including thinking and reasoning, are transformations of perceptions, feelings, needs, and memories in living beings, and that only facts deserve consideration. Sensualists deny access to contents or processes that are unexperienced or not scientifically constituted, holding that thinking and higher functions historically arise after original perception and animal desires. In this framework, Laas contrasts with Plato and Kant, who postulate a distinct faculty of reason, whereas Laas contends that epistemology and ethics should begin exclusively with experience and perception. He further contends that Kant, historically, merely replaced scholastic metaphysics with a different term, rather than effecting a genuine shift. Both sensualists and positivists tend to deny the existence of entities such as God and absolute reason, arguing that thinking, judging, and representation are grounded in sensory sensations and facts. For Laas, idealists are characterized by the claim that reason governs thought and action and can make judgments beyond what has actually been experienced.

human_text: The most successful further development of Epicurean ethics, Laas claims, was achieved by Jeremy Bentham. He expanded the sympathetic and friendly impulses of the Epicureans into a “universal philanthropy.” This individualized ethics, which Bentham calls “private ethics,” are realized in the context of the development of social policy and legislation. With that said, Laas considers Bentham's idea that ethically good actions naturally align with the prudently calculated, as if by itself, to be a mistake. Laas thinks that contemporary morality can build on the values and formulations of history. Because in general and in essence, history had the right thing in mind and, in the majority of cases, it indeed was right. But also, in contrast to Bentham, Laas adheres to the concept of duty “You shall!” "Finally, there is another argument that speaks against the morality of well-understood interest. It has a Kantian tinge, but its core and content are perfectly understandable. All serious duty comes with a categorical: Thou shalt! Who would want to give this formulation to the inspirations of prudence? It will appear as advice, not as a command; it will be hypothetical, not categorical. They will say: If you want to be happy and you find your pleasure in this course of action, more pleasure in this than in that, you will do well, etc. But why they should demand to be happy or to have pleasure in something, they cannot explain in any way. Morality must therefore either stop with its: Thou shalt! or the morality of calculation and prudence is not the true one... The first is claimed by consistent and outspoken egoists. They consider all feelings of duty to be an infatuation or foolishness. For them there is no 'Thou shalt!'... The other is our opinion. We do not believe that the whole of history up to now has been subject to a tremendous aberration, fantasy and self-deception in its moral estimations and formulations; rather, we are firmly convinced that, despite all changes and errors, it has always had the right thing in mind in general and in essence, both in its reasoning and in its detailed determinations, and that in the majority of cases it has also made the right decision. And so we remain attached to the concept of duty and the 'Thou shalt.' Not, of course, in such a way that, in the manner of Platonic morality, we only recognize duties and no rights, or that we want to allow the latter to take a disproportionate back seat to the former. On the contrary, we are inclined to give equal weight to both concepts."

He rejects the notion that ethical goodness inherently aligns with prudence, maintaining that prudent calculation and moral value can diverge. Morality, in Laas’s view, may be built on historical values, with history generally guiding toward appropriate aims and outcomes. He defends a duty-based framework, contrasting it with Bentham’s emphasis on self-interested calculation, and articulates a Kantian-tinged case that moral obligation is categorical rather than conditional on prudential outcomes. Egoists, by contrast, deny any duty, treating moral imperatives as infatuations or folly. The position advanced affirms the primacy of duty and a categorical imperative while not neglecting rights, arguing that duties and rights should be given equal weight. Platonic morality is rejected in favor of a balanced approach that harmonizes duties with rights.

It arises from events such as sonic booms or detonations and is used as a key parameter in evaluating the potential destructive effects of explosions. The concept is of particular importance in analyses concerning the effects of nuclear weapons and thermobaric devices, where higher levels of overpressure are associated with greater structural damage and human harm.

human_text: The first archaeological evidence of human occupation of Kentucky is approximately 9500 BCE, and it was Clovis culture, primitive hunter-gatherers with stone tools. Around 1800 BCE, a gradual transition began from a hunter-gatherer economy to agriculturalism. Around 900 CE, a Mississippian culture took root in western and central Kentucky and a Fort Ancient culture appeared in eastern Kentucky. While the two had many similarities, the distinctive ceremonial earthwork mounds constructed in the former's centers were not part of the culture of the latter. Fort Ancient settlements depended largely on corn, beans, and squash, and practiced a system of agriculture that prevented ecological degradation by rotating crops, burning sections of forest to create ideal habitat for wild game, relocating villages every 10–30 years, and continually shifting the location of fields to maintain plots of land in various stages of ecological succession.

human_text: Almost a year after his first abdication, Napoleon left from exile on Elba and landed on the mainland near Cannes on 1 March 1815. human_text: Consider a signal with a bandwidth or highest frequency of B = 100 Hz. The sampling theorem states that sampling frequency would have to be greater than 200 Hz. Sampling at four times that rate requires a sampling frequency of 800 Hz. This gives the anti-aliasing filter a transition band of 300 Hz ((fs/2) − B = (800 Hz/2) − 100 Hz = 300 Hz) instead of 0 Hz if the sampling frequency was 200 Hz. Achieving an anti-aliasing filter with 0 Hz transition band is unrealistic whereas an anti-aliasing filter with a transition band of 300 Hz is not difficult.
ai_text: Oversampling increases the sampling rate beyond the minimum required by the Nyquist criterion. For a signal with bandwidth B = 100 Hz, the sampling frequency must satisfy fs > 2B, i.e., exceed 200 Hz. Fourfold oversampling results in fs = 800 Hz. The anti-aliasing filter that accompanies the analog-to-digital conversion has a transition-band width equal to (fs/2) − B; with fs = 800 Hz, this computes to 400 − 100 = 300 Hz. If the system were operated at 200 Hz, the transition band would effectively be zero Hz (fs/2 − B = 100 − 100 = 0), which is impractical for real-world filters. Consequently, a transition band of about 300 Hz is feasible to implement in practice.

Even modest levels of noise can produce substantial gains in detail and accuracy. The dithering noise can be positioned outside the frequency band of interest so that it minimally affects the intended signal content. Following acquisition, the excess noise can be removed or suppressed through digital filtering, preserving the enhanced resolution while reducing noise within the targeted frequency range.

human_text: W. V. O. Quine's version of naturalized epistemology considers reasons for serious doubt about the fruitfulness of traditional philosophic study of scientific knowledge. These concerns are raised in light of the long attested incapacity of philosophers to find a satisfactory answer to the problems of radical scepticism and, more particularly, to David Hume's criticism of induction. But also, because of the contemporaneous attempts and failures to reduce mathematics to pure logic by those in or philosophically sympathetic to The Vienna Circle. Quine concludes that studies of scientific knowledge concerned with meaning or truth fail to achieve the Cartesian goal of certainty. The failures in the reduction of mathematics to pure logic imply that scientific knowledge can at best be defined with the aid of less certain set-theoretic notions. Even if set theory's lacking the certainty of pure logic is deemed acceptable, the usefulness of constructing an encoding of scientific knowledge as logic and set theory is undermined by the inability to construct a useful translation from logic and set-theory back to scientific knowledge. If no translation between scientific knowledge and the logical structures can be constructed that works both ways, then the properties of the purely logical and set-theoretic constructions do not usefully inform understanding of scientific knowledge.
ai_text: Naturalized epistemology, as articulated by Willard Van Orman Quine, questions the fruitfulness of traditional philosophy of science. Its critique rests on the long-standing failure of philosophers to resolve radical skepticism and Hume’s problem of induction, and it is intensified by the Vienna Circle’s program to reduce mathematics to pure logic, a program Quine contends has not succeeded. He argues that analyses of meaning or truth within science do not accomplish the Cartesian goal of achieving absolute certainty. The unsuccessful reduction of mathematics to logic further implies that scientific knowledge must be described using set-theoretic notions that come with a lower degree of epistemic certainty. Even if one accepts some instability in set theory, attempting to encode scientific knowledge purely as logic or set theory is undermined by the absence of a useful translation back to substantive scientific content. Consequently, without a bidirectional translation between scientific knowledge and formal logical structures, the properties of logic or set theory fail to illuminate our understanding of science.

human_text: Metro Rail began service on July 14, 1990, when the light rail Blue Line opened between Pico and Anaheim Street stations; the line was extended to Downtown Long Beach and Pacific Avenue stations on September 1. The Blue Line was extended one stop northward from Pico to 7th Street/Metro Center on February 15, 1991. The next Metro Rail line, the rapid transit Red Line, opened on January 30, 1993, between Union Station and Westlake/​MacArthur Park station. The light rail Green Line, the system's third line, opened on August 12, 1995, from Norwalk to Redondo Beach stations. Metro Rail's next expansion occurred on May 22, 1996, when the Red Line expanded westward from Westlake/MacArthur Park to Wilshire/​Western stations. The Red Line expanded again on June 12, 1999, with a branch from Wilshire/​Vermont to Hollywood/Vine stations. The final section of the Red Line opened on June 24, 2000, from Hollywood/Vine station to North Hollywood station, completing the Red Line as originally planned. A fourth Metro Rail line, the light rail Gold Line, opened on July 27, 2003, between Union Station and Sierra Madre Villa station in Pasadena. The rapid transit Purple Line became the fifth Metro Rail line on August 24, 2006, when Los Angeles Metro separated the Red Line into two separate services; the branch between Union Station and Wilshire/Western station became the Purple Line while the branch between Union Station and North Hollywood station remained the Red Line. The Gold Line was later extended to Atlantic station in East Los Angeles on November 15, 2009. The light rail Expo Line opened between 7th Street/Metro Center and La Cienega/Jefferson on April 28, 2012; two additional stations opened on June 20, 2012. The Gold Line's second extension opened on March 5, 2016, and added six more stations from Sierra Madre Villa from to APU/Citrus College. An extension to the Expo Line on May 20, 2016, added seven stations. The opening of the K Line on October 7, 2022, added six stations. The Regional Connector project featured two new underground stations as well as a rebuilt Little Tokyo/Arts District station. Aviation/Century station opened on November 3, 2024. The LAX/Metro Transit Center opened on June 6, 2025. The first phase of the A Line Foothill Extension, consisting of four new stations and 9.1 mi (14.6 km) of track, opened on September 19, 2025.

human_text: Assuming perfect combustion conditions, such as complete combustion under adiabatic conditions (i.e., no heat loss or gain), the adiabatic combustion temperature can be determined. The formula that yields this temperature is based on the first law of thermodynamics and takes note of the fact that the heat of combustion is used entirely for heating the fuel, the combustion air or oxygen, and the combustion product gases (commonly referred to as the flue gas).
ai_text: Perfect combustion refers to the complete oxidation of the fuel with the oxidizer under adiabatic conditions, meaning no heat is exchanged with the surroundings. Under these idealized circumstances, the adiabatic combustion temperature, often called the adiabatic flame temperature, can be determined by applying an energy balance derived from the first law of thermodynamics. In such analyses, the chemical energy released by combustion is assumed to be wholly devoted to heating the fuel, the combustion air or oxygen, and the combustion product gases, collectively referred to as the flue gas. Consequently, the final temperature is obtained by equating the heat of reaction to the sum of the sensible heats of all species at the final state, a calculation that depends on the fuel–oxidizer mixture, initial temperatures, and the heat capacities of the participating substances.

ai_text: The ecological role of Tyrannosaurus rex—whether it functioned primarily as a predator or as a scavenger—has been a subject of ongoing debate. The discussion traces back to Lawrence Lambe's 1917 analysis, which argued that large theropods might have been mainly scavengers, citing the apparent lack of tooth wear on Gorgosaurus as evidence. That interpretation overlooked the fact that theropod dentition was rapidly replaced, a feature that could mask wear even in active feeders. Since the initial discovery of Tyrannosaurus, most researchers have favored a predatory lifestyle, consistent with its cranial morphology and biomechanics. Nevertheless, as with many contemporary apex predators, Tyrannosaurus would likely have scavenged or stolen kills when the opportunity arose, reflecting an opportunistic feeding strategy rather than a strict classification as either hunter or scavenger.

human_text: The instrument used to detect the Cherenkov radiation usually comprises a large segmented mirror which reflects the Cherenkov light onto an array of photomultiplier tubes. The tubes are coupled to fast electronics which amplify, digitise and record the pattern or image of the shower. The most effective mode of operation is to use an array of such telescopes, which can be typically located 70 to 120 meters apart. The primary advantage of this mode of operation is that the energy threshold (the peak sensitivity) of the telescope can be lowered as local muons produced by cosmic ray induced showers can be eliminated. This is because the narrow Cherenkov light cone produced by local muons will only be recorded by a single telescope. The shower reconstruction and background rejection offered by an array of telescopes provides an order of magnitude increase in sensitivity and improved angular and energy resolution as compared to a single telescope. This advantage has been used to great effect by the H.E.S.S. telescope array which has detected several new sources of very high energy gamma-ray photons in recent years.

The PMTs are connected to fast electronics that amplify, digitize, and record the resulting shower image. The most effective observational approach employs a network of telescopes spaced roughly 70 to 120 meters apart, enabling stereoscopic views of the air showers. The array configuration also lowers the energy threshold by discriminating against local muon events, whose narrow Cherenkov light cones are typically captured by a single telescope. Array-based shower reconstruction and background rejection provide about an order of magnitude improvement in sensitivity and yield better angular and energy resolution compared with a single telescope. This advantage has been demonstrated by the H.E.S.S. telescope array, which has used it to detect several new sources of very high energy gamma-ray photons in recent years.

human_text: Vishishtadvaita, propounded by Ramanuja (11–12th century), asserts that Jīvatman (human souls) and Brahman (as Vishnu) are different, a difference that is never transcended. With this qualification, Ramanuja also affirmed monism by saying that there is unity of all souls and that the individual soul has the potential to realize identity with the Brahman. Vishishtadvaita is a qualified non-dualistic school of Vedanta and like Advaita, begins by assuming that all souls can hope for and achieve the state of blissful liberation. On the relation between the Brahman and the world of matter (Prakriti), Vishishtadvaita states both are two different absolutes, both metaphysically true and real, neither is false or illusive, and that saguna Brahman with attributes is also real. Ramanuja states that God, like man, has both soul and body, and the world of matter is the glory of God's body. The path to Brahman (Vishnu), according to Ramanuja, is devotion to godliness and constant remembrance of the beauty and love of the personal god (bhakti of saguna Brahman).
ai_text: Vishishtadvaita, a sub-school of Vedanta articulated by Ramanuja in the 11th–12th centuries, holds that individual souls (jivatman) and Brahman (identified with Vishnu) are fundamentally distinct, a difference that remains permanent rather than transcended. It also asserts the unity of all souls and teaches that the individual soul can realize its identity with Brahman within a framework of qualified monism. As a form of qualified non-dualism, it maintains that liberation is achievable for all beings, and like Advaita Vedanta, it posits that both Brahman and Prakriti (the world) are real and absolutes, not illusory, with saguna Brahman (God with attributes) likewise real. God is conceived as possessing both soul and body, and the material universe is described as the manifestation of God’s body. The path to Brahman (Vishnu) lies in devotion (bhakti) to the personal deity, accompanied by constant remembrance of his beauty and love. Accordingly, bhakti directed toward saguna Brahman is presented as the means to liberation.

human_text: As a purely intraframe compression scheme, the image quality of M-JPEG is directly a function of each video frame's static (spatial) complexity. Frames with large smooth transitions or monotone surfaces compress well and are more likely to hold their original details with few visible compression artifacts. Frames exhibiting complex textures, fine curves and lines (such as writing on a newspaper) are prone to exhibit discrete cosine transform (DCT) artifacts such as ringing, smudging and macroblocking. M-JPEG-compressed video is also insensitive to motion complexity, i.e. variation over time. It is neither hindered by highly random motion (such as the water-surface turbulence in a large waterfall), nor helped by the absence of motion (such as static landscape shot by tripod), which are two opposite extremes commonly used to test interframe video formats.
ai_text: Motion JPEG (M-JPEG) encodes each frame separately using intraframe compression, with no dependencies between frames. As a result, image quality is governed primarily by the spatial complexity of individual frames rather than by motion or temporal variation. Smooth and monotone frames typically compress well and preserve details with relatively few artifacts. By contrast, frames containing intricate textures or fine lines—such as text—can exhibit discrete cosine transform artifacts, including ringing, smudging, and macroblocking. The absence of interframe references means temporal variation has little impact on quality. In testing video formats, extreme cases of random motion and static scenes are often used to stress interframe codecs, but M-JPEG is not hindered by these extremes.

ai_text: Motion JPEG encodes each frame as an individual JPEG image; however, its efficiency has become limited relative to modern video codecs. Several later standards replace or augment JPEG-style coding with more effective techniques. For example, H.263v2 Annex I and MPEG-4 Part 2 apply frequency-domain prediction of transform coefficients, while H.264/MPEG-4 AVC uses spatial prediction and adaptive transform block sizes to better exploit redundancy. In addition, entropy coding has grown more sophisticated since JPEG's original design. Taken together, these developments render Motion JPEG an inefficient recording mechanism compared with newer standards.

human_text: The modern theory that explains the nature of light includes the notion of wave–particle duality. The theory is based on the concept that every quantum entity can show wave-like or particle-like behaviors, depending on observation. The observation led to the collapse of the entity's wave function. If it is based on the Copenhagen interpretation, the observation does really collapse the wave function; for the many-worlds interpretation, all possible outcomes of the collapse happened in parallel universes; for the pilot wave theory, the particle behaviour is simply determined by waves. The duality nature of a real photon has been observed in the double-slit experiment.
ai_text: Electromagnetic radiation is traditionally described by classical waves, but quantum theory treats light as exhibiting wave–particle duality, a central concept in understanding its nature. Quantum objects such as photons can display wave-like or particle-like properties depending on the experimental arrangement, underscoring how observation influences outcomes. In the Copenhagen interpretation, measurement causes the quantum state to collapse to a definite result, whereas the many-worlds interpretation contends that all possible results are realized in branching, parallel universes. A further approach, pilot-wave theory, holds that particle motion is guided deterministically by an accompanying wave. The dual character of single photons has been demonstrated in the double-slit experiment, which reveals interference patterns alongside detected particle events.

human_text: OPEC members strongly prefer to describe their organisation as a modest force for market stabilisation, rather than a powerful anti-competitive cartel. In its defense, the organisation was founded as a counterweight against the previous "Seven Sisters" cartel of multinational oil companies, and non-OPEC energy suppliers have maintained enough market share for a substantial degree of worldwide competition. Moreover, because of an economic "prisoner's dilemma" that encourages each member nation individually to discount its price and exceed its production quota, widespread cheating within OPEC often erodes its ability to influence global oil prices through collective action. Political scientist Jeff Colgan has challenged the notion that OPEC is a cartel, pointing to endemic cheating in the organization: "A cartel needs to set tough goals and meet them; OPEC sets easy goals and fails to meet even those."

Non-OPEC producers retain substantial market shares, preserving ongoing competitive pressure in the global oil market. In practice, a prisoner’s dilemma among members encourages underpricing and production beyond quotas, producing widespread noncompliance that weakens OPEC’s ability to influence prices. Some analysts, notably Jeff Colgan, question the cartel label, arguing that cheating is endemic; he contends that a true cartel should set stringent goals and meet them, whereas OPEC tends to adopt relatively easy targets and falls short of meeting even those.

After that war, most mortars settled on the Stokes pattern, characterized by a short barrel, smooth bore, low muzzle velocity, elevation angle of firing generally greater than 45°, and a very simple and light mounting using a "baseplate" on the ground. The modern mortar originated during World War I, when several patterns were developed, and in the postwar period the Stokes pattern became the standard design. The Stokes pattern is defined by a short, smooth-bore barrel, low muzzle velocity, and a lightweight baseplate that sits on the ground, with elevation typically greater than 45 degrees. Ammunition is designed for drop-fire: the projectile contains its own propellant charge and is dropped down the barrel from the muzzle to strike a fixed firing pin. Since then, a minority of mortars have been produced with rifled barrels and breech-loading capabilities.

human_text: The 52-bar long motet in F major is scored SATB choir and S and A soloists, organ and cello (continuo). It begins in Andante with a fugato. The fugato is ending on bar 8 with the by Haas so-called Marien-Kadenz (cadence on the word "Maria"), which Bruckner will recall in the first movement of the Study Symphony in F minor and in the Adagio of the later Symphony No. 3. On the next bar the alto soloist is singing "gratia plena" and on bar 13 the soprano soloist is going on with "benedicta tu". On bars 18-22 the score is slowing down to Adagio, during which the choir is singing three times "Jesus". Bruckner will repeat this three times "Jesus" in his next two settings of the Ave Maria. The second part of the motet is sung by the choir (bars 23-52). The score, which goes back to Andante, begins with "Sancta Maria", sung in canon and ends with the beginning motif.

The work proceeds at Andante and features a fugato texture, culminating the opening eight bars with a Marien-Kadenz cadence on the word Maria. This cadence is later recalled by Bruckner in the first movement of his Study Symphony in F minor and in the Adagio of his Symphony No. 3. Bar 9 introduces the alto solo with the text gratia plena, and bar 13 presents the soprano solo with benedicta tu. Between bars 18 and 22 the pace slows to Adagio, during which the choir voices the word Jesus three times; this threefold invocation of Jesus is a motif Bruckner repeats in his two subsequent Ave Maria settings. The second section, bars 23 through 52, is sung by the choir; the texture returns to Andante, opening this part with Sancta Maria sung in canon, and the piece ends by returning to the initial motif.

human_text: The 1850 census had a dramatic shift in the way information about residents was collected. For the first time, free persons were listed individually instead of by head of household. Two questionnaires were used – one for free inhabitants and one for slaves. The question on the free inhabitants schedule about color was a column that was to be left blank if a person were white, marked "B" if a person were black, and marked "M" if a person were mulatto. Slaves were listed by owner, and classified by gender and age, not individually, and the question about color was a column that was to be marked with a "B" if the slave were black and an "M" if mulatto.

Enslaved people were listed under the ownership of a master rather than as separate individuals, and their entries were categorized by sex and age. In this slave schedule, the color field similarly used "B" for black and "M" for mulatto.

This expansion of luxury consumption in England was facilitated by state policies that encouraged cultural borrowing and import substitution, hence enabling the purchase of luxury items. Luxury goods included sugar, tobacco, tea, and coffee; these were increasingly grown on vast plantations (historically by slave labor) in the Caribbean as demand steadily rose. In particular, sugar consumption in Britain increased by a factor of 20 during the 18th century.

human_text: Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253), also known as Origen Adamantius, was an early Christian scholar, ascetic, and theologian who was born and spent the first half of his career in Alexandria. He was a prolific writer who wrote roughly 2,000 treatises in multiple branches of theology, including textual criticism, biblical exegesis and hermeneutics, homiletics, and spirituality. He was one of the most influential and controversial figures in early Christian theology, apologetics, and asceticism. He has been described by John Anthony McGuckin as "the greatest genius the early church ever produced".

While teaching in Caesarea, Origen resumed work on his Commentary on John, composing at least books six through ten. In the first of these books, Origen compares himself to "an Israelite who has escaped the perverse persecution of the Egyptians". Origen also wrote the treatise On Prayer at the request of his friend Ambrose and Tatiana (referred to as the "sister" of Ambrose), in which he analyzes the different types of prayers described in the Bible and offers a detailed exegesis on the Lord's Prayer.

human_text: There are two general strategies for searching a federation of digital libraries: distributed searching and searching previously harvested metadata.
ai_text: In the context of a federation of digital libraries, search functionality must span multiple repositories to locate materials across diverse collections. One common strategy is distributed searching, wherein a query is sent to several member libraries and the resulting records are collected and merged to present a unified result set, often with deduplication and ranking. A second approach involves searching metadata that has been harvested from the participating libraries and indexed locally, enabling rapid, centralized access to descriptions and links to the original sources. Each method carries trade-offs: distributed searching can offer up-to-date results but may incur higher latency and coordination complexity, while harvested metadata allows faster searches at the expense of potentially stale records if harvesting intervals are infrequent. Hybrid configurations may combine both techniques to improve breadth, currency, and performance.

human_text: The Digital Millennium Copyright Act of 1998 was an act created in the United States to attempt to deal with the introduction of digital works. This Act incorporates two treaties from the year 1996. It criminalizes the attempt to circumvent measures which limit access to copyrighted materials. It also criminalizes the act of attempting to circumvent access control. This act provides an exemption for nonprofit libraries and archives which allows up to three copies to be made, one of which may be digital. This may not be made public or distributed on the web, however. Further, it allows libraries and archives to copy a work if its format becomes obsolete.

They established a bakery business in Avarua. On May 12, 1942, the Cook Islands first converts, Samuel Glassie and his family, were baptized. human_text: In a battery electric vehicle, there are usually two separate DC systems. The "high voltage" system operates at 300-400V (depending on the vehicle), and provides the power for the traction motors. Increasing the voltage for the traction motors reduces the current flowing through them, increasing efficiency.

Increasing the traction voltage for a given motor power reduces the current drawn, thereby improving overall efficiency by lowering electrical losses.

human_text: In a DC circuit, a power source (e.g. a battery, capacitor, etc.) has a positive and negative terminal, and likewise, the load also has a positive and negative terminal. To complete the circuit, positive charges need to flow from the power source to the load. The charges will then return to the negative terminal of the load, which will then flow back to the negative terminal of the battery, completing the circuit. If either the positive or negative terminal is disconnected, the circuit will not be complete and the charges will not flow.
ai_text: In a direct current circuit, both the power source and the load possess positive and negative terminals. Conventional current flows from the power source’s positive terminal through the load and back to the source’s negative terminal, thereby forming a closed loop. If either terminal becomes disconnected, the circuit is opened and the flow of charges ceases.

human_text: The Ljung–Box test (named for Greta M. Ljung and George E. P. Box) is a type of statistical test of whether any of a group of autocorrelations of a time series are different from zero. ai_text: The Ljung–Box test, named after Greta M. Ljung and George E. P. Box, is a statistical procedure used to determine whether any of a group of autocorrelations of a time series differ from zero. Rather than evaluating each lag separately, it tests the joint hypothesis that the autocorrelations up to a chosen number of lags are collectively zero, thereby assessing overall randomness across multiple lags. As a portmanteau test, it combines information across lags into a single statistic to gauge lack of fit or randomness in the data.

human_text: A programming tool or software development tool is a computer program that is used to develop another computer program, usually by helping the developer manage computer files. Examples include source code editors, which provide facilities for editing source text, and compilers, which translate high-level code into machine-readable executables. Build tools extend these capabilities by automating the packaging of software components into distributable bundles, combining executables and data files into installable kits or installers.

human_text: A set of tools that are run one after another, with each tool feeding its output to the next one, is called a toolchain. Most IDEs include a source code editor as a core component, and they typically offer built-in or extensible features to assist with compiling, debugging, and testing, either natively or through plug-ins.

human_text: Daily life in a Tongva village was structured around communal and familial activities. Tongva dwellings (called kich or kiiğa) were dome-shaped structures made of willow branches and thatched with tule or other grasses. These homes had a central fire pit and a smoke hole at the top for ventilation. Villages typically ranged from a few dozen to a hundred people, and early Spanish observers noted that each village was politically autonomous under its own chief, yet linked to others by kinship and language. Men and women both had important economic roles: men often did most of the hunting and fishing, while women were expert foragers and skilled in processing plant foods and weaving baskets. Both sexes wore their hair long and adorned their bodies with tattoos and paint. Clothing was minimal in the warm Southern California climate—men often wore little more than a breechcloth, and women wore skirts made of deer hide or woven fiber. In cooler weather, they draped themselves in capes or cloaks made from animal skins, and sandals woven from yucca fiber or hide protected their feet. Tongva spiritual life was rich, with ceremonies marking events like the summer solstice and communal mourning rituals for the dead. They had deep knowledge of local plants for food, medicine, and materials, reflecting a relationship with the land that was both practical and spiritual.

human_text: Peter Self criticizes the traditional socialist planned economy and argues against pursuing "extreme equality" because he believes it requires "strong coercion" and does not allow for "reasonable recognition [for] different individual needs, tastes (for work or leisure) and talents". Self holds that while a socialist planned economy provides substantially greater freedom than is present in capitalism—under which the vast majority of people are coerced by the threat of starvation to work for the profit of a small capitalist class—adding markets to socialism improves freedom and efficiency. Accordingly, Self recommends market socialism instead of either capitalism or non-market socialism. Philosopher David Schweickart has described similar views.
ai_text: Anti-socialist is a position associated with the political economist Peter Self, who critiques the traditional socialist planned economy. Self argues that pursuing extreme equality risks coercive enforcement and fails to recognize the diverse needs, tastes, and talents of individuals in work and leisure. He maintains that a socialist planned economy can confer substantially greater freedom than capitalism, countering the view that socialism inherently restricts liberty. He further contends that capitalism exerts coercion on the majority by compelling them to work to sustain a small capitalist class. To address these tensions, Self proposes introducing market elements into socialism, arguing that such hybrids can enhance both freedom and efficiency. Therefore, market socialism is presented as an alternative to both capitalism and non-market socialism. Philosopher David Schweickart has described views similar to Self’s.

human_text: The converse can be proven as well: if a formula always has the value 1, then it is deducible from the laws of intuitionistic logic, so the intuitionistically valid formulas are exactly those that always have a value of 1. This is similar to the notion that classically valid formulas are those formulas that have a value of 1 in the two-element Boolean algebra under any possible assignment of true and false to the formula's variables—that is, they are formulas that are tautologies in the usual truth-table sense. A Heyting algebra, from the logical standpoint, is then a generalization of the usual system of truth values, and its largest element 1 is analogous to 'true'. The usual two-valued logic system is a special case of a Heyting algebra, and the smallest non-trivial one, in which the only elements of the algebra are 1 (true) and 0 (false).
ai_text: A Heyting algebra provides an abstract setting for reasoning about truth values in intuitionistic logic, generalizing the familiar Boolean truth-value system by having a designated top element 1 that stands for truth. In this framework, a formula is intuitionistically valid precisely when it evaluates to 1 under every interpretation, and such formulas are exactly those that are deducible from the laws of intuitionistic logic. By contrast, formulas that are classically valid are those that evaluate to 1 under all variable assignments in the two-element Boolean algebra, i.e., tautologies. The usual two-valued logic is encompassed as a special case of a Heyting algebra, showing how classical results fit within the broader intuitionistic setting. The simplest non-trivial example of a Heyting algebra comprises just two elements, 1 and 0, corresponding to true and false. In this way, Heyting algebras provide a structured generalization of truth values with a clear connection to both intuitionistic deduction and classical tautologies.

human_text: An arcus cloud is a low, horizontal cloud formation, usually appearing as an accessory cloud to a cumulonimbus. Roll clouds and shelf clouds are the two main types of arcus clouds. They most frequently form along the leading edge or gust fronts of thunderstorms; some of the most dramatic arcus formations mark the gust fronts of derecho-producing convective systems. Roll clouds may also arise in the absence of thunderstorms, forming along the shallow cold air currents of some sea breeze boundaries and cold fronts.

Roll clouds, in particular, may form even in the absence of thunderstorms, arising from shallow cold air currents associated with sea breeze boundaries and cold fronts.

human_text: Patients with Lyme disease who are treated with appropriate antibiotics usually recover rapidly and completely. Antibiotics commonly used include doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime axetil. For Anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, and Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, Doxycycline is the first-line treatment for adults and children of all ages. For babesiosis, a combination therapy with atovaquone and azithromycin is most commonly recommended for the treatment of mild to moderate babesiosis. Treatment is usually continued for 7 to 10 days. A combination regimen of oral clindamycin and quinine has also been proven effective, but the rate of adverse reactions is significantly higher with this combination. For the Powassan virus, there are no medications for treating Powassan virus infections. Medications, however, can help to relieve symptoms and prevent complications. People with severe disease are typically treated in a hospital where they may be given intravenous fluids, fever-reducing medications, breathing support, and other therapies as needed.

human_text: The Great Powers sought to re-assert control through the 1913 Treaty of London, which had created an independent Albania while enlarging the territories of Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro and Greece. However, disputes between the victors sparked the 33-day Second Balkan War, when Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece on 16 June 1913; it was defeated, losing most of Macedonia to Serbia and Greece, and Southern Dobruja to Romania. The result was that even countries which benefited from the Balkan Wars, such as Serbia and Greece, felt cheated of their "rightful gains", while for Austria it demonstrated the apparent indifference with which other powers viewed their concerns, including Germany. This complex mix of resentment, nationalism and insecurity helps explain why the pre-1914 Balkans became known as the "powder keg of Europe".

However, disagreements among the victors over these gains sparked a brief but decisive conflict known as the Second Balkan War, which began when Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece on 16 June 1913. Bulgaria was defeated in this 33‑day conflict, losing most of its Macedonian holdings to Serbia and Greece, and Southern Dobruja to Romania. As the outcomes disappointed the states that had benefited from the initial settlements, Serbia and Greece in particular felt shortchanged, while Austria-Hungary observed what it perceived as evident indifference from other powers, including Germany. This combination of lingering resentment, rising nationalism, and general insecurity in the pre‑war Balkans contributed to the region being characterized as a powder keg of Europe, signaling the volatile environment that helped propel the broader conflict of World War I.

human_text: A proposal of work (New Proposal) is approved at the Subcommittee level and then at the Technical Committee level (SC 29 and JTC 1, respectively, in the case of MPEG). When the scope of new work is sufficiently clarified, MPEG usually makes open "calls for proposals". The first document that is produced for audio and video coding standards is typically called a test model. When a sufficient confidence in the stability of the standard under development is reached, a Working Draft (WD) is produced. When a WD is sufficiently solid (typically after producing several numbered WDs), the next draft is issued as a Committee Draft (CD) (usually at the planned time) and is sent to National Bodies (NBs) for comment. When a consensus is reached to proceed to the next stage, the draft becomes a Draft International Standard (DIS) and is sent for another ballot. After a review and comments issued by NBs and a resolution of comments in the working group, a Final Draft International Standard (FDIS) is typically issued for a final approval ballot. The final approval ballot is voted on by National Bodies, with no technical changes allowed (a yes/no approval ballot). If approved, the document becomes an International Standard (IS). In cases where the text is considered sufficiently mature, the WD, CD, and/or FDIS stages can be skipped. The development of a standard is completed when the FDIS document has been issued, with the FDIS stage only being for final approval, and in practice, the FDIS stage for MPEG standards has always resulted in approval.

Due to the geopolitical climate of the Middle East, urbanization has caused many of the nomadic cultures and rural regions to cluster or move altogether. This has brought more modernized musical instruments and oral poetry together which collaborate and are currently played throughout regions of the Middle East.

human_text: Augustinerkirche was once one of the five main churches in the medieval town of Zürich. In 1841 the Roman Catholic community of Zürich planned to rebuild the building to commemorate the old Augustinian church. But, as the majority of the Catholic community rejected the decisions of the First Vatican Council of 1870, the whole community was expelled from the Catholic church. For the same reason, Augustinerkirche is still their parish church. Today the building is one of the three medieval churches in the Lindenhof district of the city of Zürich.

human_text: A crib lighthouse is a type of lighthouse whose structure rests on a concrete or masonry foundation supported with wooden beams. When it came time to build, wooden cribs were constructed onshore then towed to the site where they were filled with stone so they sank in place. Problems arose however if the crib settled unevenly into the earth as was the case with the Detroit River Light.

John Luther Adams writes music directly from his surroundings in Alaska. He is an environmentalist who has written and discussed the role that artists can play in combating global warming. ai_text: In the decades following World War II, modern classical music increasingly drew inspiration from the natural world, weaving ecological motifs and field-derived sounds into compositional practice. Cage’s work Child of Tree exemplifies this direction by foregrounding environmental sounds and incorporating unconventional sound-producing elements—such as a cactus and a pea pod shaker—alongside other instruments selected by the performer, thereby broadening the traditional sonic palette. John Luther Adams, meanwhile, composes from his surroundings in Alaska and positions himself as an environmentalist who argues that artists have a role in addressing global warming. His sound-and-light installation The Place Where You Go to Listen reflects this ethos by being controlled by natural events as they occur in real time, linking sensory perception with environmental processes and technology.

human_text: The King Alfred Chair of English Literature was founded at the University of Liverpool, England in 1881. It was one of the original endowments of the University, funded by William Rathbone and his brothers Samuel and Phillip Rathbone. The early history of the chair was as follows: King Alfred Chair of Modern History and Literature, 1881–82; Modern Literature and History, 1882-1884; Modern Literature and English Language, 1884-1900.

In its early history the chair’s designation and remit underwent changes, with the title listed as the King Alfred Chair of Modern History and Literature for 1881–82, then Modern Literature and History from 1882–84, and subsequently Modern Literature and English Language from 1884–1900.

ai_text: Glass making relies on raw materials that are typically delivered as dusty powders or fine-grained substances. Maintaining effective dust-control systems in such facilities is challenging, given the nature of the materials and processes. The large daily throughput of materials means that even a small release of dust can create operational difficulties. In addition, cullet, consisting of broken or waste glass, is circulated around the plant, and handling it—whether by shoveling or breaking—tends to generate fine glass particles.

human_text: The notation is analogous with that for an inverse function. Although many functions do not have an inverse, every relation does have a unique converse. The unary operation that maps a relation to the converse relation is an involution, so it induces the structure of a semigroup with involution on the binary relations on a set, or, more generally, induces a dagger category on the category of relations as detailed below. As a unary operation, taking the converse (sometimes called conversion or transposition) commutes with the order-related operations of the calculus of relations, that is it commutes with union, intersection, and complement.
ai_text: Converse relation denotes the transpose of a relation and is analogous to the notation used for inverse functions. While not every relation possesses an inverse in the sense of a function, each relation has a unique converse obtained by reversing the order of its ordered pairs. The converse is a unary operation that is an involution, since applying it twice returns the original relation. This operation endows the set of binary relations on a given set with a semigroup structure equipped with involution, and more broadly it endows the category of relations with the structure of a dagger category. In the calculus of relations, the converse commutes with the standard operations of union, intersection, and complement.

human_text: A function is invertible if and only if its converse relation is a function, in which case the converse relation is the inverse function.
ai_text: In mathematics, the converse (or inverse) of a relation R ⊆ X×Y is the relation R^−1 = { (y, x) | (x, y) ∈ R }. When R is the graph of a function f: X → Y, its converse is a relation from Y to X; the function f is invertible if and only if this converse relation is itself a function, in which case it serves as the inverse function f^−1: Y → X. Conversely, if the converse is not a function, the original function is not invertible, since a given y would correspond to multiple x values.

ai_text: The United States Air Force maintains a peacetime organizational framework tasked with organizing, equipping, and training air units for planned operational missions. When called upon to execute actual operations, the Secretary of Defense directs the Secretary of the Air Force to implement a Change in Operational Control, transferring units from their administrative alignment to the operational command of a regional Combatant Command. In practice, units assigned to Air Force Space Command, Air Force Special Operations Command, Pacific Air Forces, and United States Air Forces in Europe are typically employed under their existing Combatant Commanders, remaining under their current regional CCDR. Air Mobility Command forces that provide support retain compositional control under United States Transportation Command unless they are CHOPped to a regional CCDR. This arrangement supports peacetime readiness and provides a mechanism for centralized control during joint operations across theaters.

ai_text: Dedicated outdoor air systems (DOAS) deliver outdoor air independently of the primary heating and cooling equipment to meet ventilation requirements, while leaving the space-conditioning system to manage temperature and humidity. In VAV installations that follow ASHRAE 62.1-2004 multi-space calculations, the outdoor-air requirement is typically 20–70 percent higher than the amount provided by a DOAS to ensure proper distribution of air within occupied spaces. The process of cooling and dehumidifying the large outdoor-air volumes in summer and humidifying and heating them in winter is energy-intensive. Accordingly, a DOAS is sized to meet the outdoor-air requirements without the need for oversizing.

human_text: Nouns decline for five cases: nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, instrumental; three genders: masculine, feminine, neuter; and two numbers: singular, and plural; and are strong or weak. The instrumental is vestigial and only used with the masculine and neuter singular and often replaced by the dative. Only pronouns and strong adjectives retain separate instrumental forms. There is also sparse early Northumbrian evidence of a sixth case: the locative. The evidence comes from Northumbrian Runic texts (e.g. ᚩᚾ ᚱᚩᛞᛁ on rodi 'on the Cross').
ai_text: Old English nouns are declined across five cases—nominative, accusative, genitive, dative, and instrumental—distinguishing three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) and two numbers (singular and plural). They are traditionally divided into strong and weak declensions, with the instrumental largely vestigial and used only in masculine and neuter singular forms, frequently replaced by the dative in normal usage. By contrast, pronouns and strong adjectives retain distinct instrumental forms. There is only sparse early evidence for a sixth locative case in Northumbrian sources, with the locative being inferred from Northumbrian Runic inscriptions, such as readings like “on rodi,” interpreted as “on the Cross.”

human_text: Old English literacy developed after the Christianisation of Anglo-Saxon England in the late 7th century. There is a limited corpus of runic inscriptions from the 5th to 7th centuries, but the oldest coherent runic texts (notably the inscriptions on the Franks Casket) date to the early 8th century. The Old English Latin alphabet was introduced around the 8th century.
ai_text: Following the Christianisation of Anglo-Saxon England in the late seventh century, literacy in Old English expanded through monastic scholarship and ecclesiastical networks. The oldest surviving Old English composition is Cædmon's Hymn, believed to have been composed between 658 and 680 and later preserved in writing during the early eighth century. The surviving runic material from this period is limited, with inscriptions spanning the fifth to seventh centuries; the earliest coherent runic texts appear in the early eighth century, among which the Franks Casket inscriptions are particularly notable. Around the same time, Old English began to be written with the Latin alphabet, which was introduced in the eighth century.

human_text: The Nazi salute, also known as the Hitler salute, or the Sieg Heil salute, is a gesture that was used as a greeting in Nazi Germany. The salute is usually accompanied by a cry of "Heil Hitler!" ('Hail Hitler!'), "Heil, mein Führer!" ('Hail, my leader!'), or "Sieg Heil!" ('Hail victory!').

human_text: Metal screwpiles were used to form the foundation of many lighthouses built on sandy or muddy bottoms. The helicoidal or screw-like cast-iron flange at the end of the metal pile was augured into the bottom increasing the bearing capacity of the pile as well as its anchoring properties. Yet lighthouses built with these foundations were found to be vulnerable to ice floes. In areas such as the Florida Keys, where the bottom is soft coral rock, diskpile foundation lighthouses were built. Wrought iron piles were driven through a cast-iron or semi-steel disk which rested on the sea floor until a shoulder on the pile prevented further penetration. The disk distributes the weight of the tower more evenly over the bottom. In coral reef areas where sand is also prevalent, a cast-steel screw was fitted to the end of the pile to give it more anchoring ability. Cofferdams were used generally in shallow waters where it was not necessary to deeply penetrate the natural bottom. The cofferdam enabled the water inside the dam to be pumped out and the foundation built "in the dry".

During the Risorgimento, the cry Viva VERDI circulated as a public expression of support for Italian unification; the phrase is commonly read as an acronym for Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re d'Italia, underscoring loyalty to Victor Emmanuel II, the reigning king. Through these associations, Verdi's music is understood to have contributed to nationalist feeling by linking art with political aspirations and the broader project of unification.

As the founder of the Georgian Philharmonic Society and later the head of the Tbilisi State Conservatoire, he played a central role in developing Georgia’s musical institutions and education. His compositions are regarded as providing the basis for the Georgian National Anthem, illustrating the enduring impact of his work on the nation’s cultural and symbolic life.

human_text: A bent or indirect entrance is a defensive feature in medieval fortification. In a castle with a bent entrance, the gate passage is narrow and turns sharply. Its purpose is to slow down attackers attempting to rush the gate and impede the use of battering rams against doors. It is often combined with means for an active defence, such as machicolations, in effect confining intruders to a narrow killing zone. Its defensive function is related to that of a barbican in front of the gate.

human_text: Prominent bulbs of force generally indicate that a hard hammer percussor (hammerstone) was used to detach the flake; flakes displaying this characteristic are referred to as conchoidal flakes. Hard hammer flakes are indicative of primary reduction strategies (e.g., core reduction, roughing of blanks and preforms, and the like). More moderate and diffuse bulbs may indicate the use of a soft hammer percussor—such as bone, wood, or antler—which produces the bending flakes often associated with bifacial thinning and trimming. The relative abundance of each type of flake can indicate what sort of lithic work was going on at a particular spot at a particular point in time.
ai_text: Flake morphology provides insight into the percussion technology used during lithic reduction. Pronounced bulbs of force signal hard hammer percussion, typically from a hammerstone, and the resulting flakes are commonly described as conchoidal. Hard-hammer flaking is generally associated with initial reduction stages, including core reduction and the rough shaping of blanks or preforms. By contrast, softer percussors such as bone, wood, or antler produce more moderate and diffuse bulbs of percussion, yielding bending flakes that are often linked to bifacial thinning and trimming. The relative frequency of hard- and soft-hammer flakes at a site or surface helps reconstruct the dominant lithic activities and tempo of production at that place and period.

human_text: The striking platform is the point on the proximal portion of the flake on which the detachment blow fell or pressure was placed. This may be natural or prepared. Termination type is a characteristic indicating the manner in which the distal end of a flake detached from a core. Flake terminations may be feathered, hinged, stepped, or plunging (also known as overshot or outrepassé). Feathered terminations are often very sharp, as the flake gradually reduces to a very fine thickness before the force exits the core and removes the flake. Hinged terminations are the result of the force rolling away from the core, resulting in a rounded distal end. Step terminations result when a flake prematurely breaks or snaps during removal, leaving a distal end that is often squared off. Plunging flakes are the result of the force rolling back towards the core and often taking off its "bottom". Hinge, step, and plunging terminations, although sometimes deliberately formed, are usually errors called "abrupt terminations". Abrupt terminations are often indicative of internal flaws in a core or previously formed Hertzian cones on the surface. Eraillures, also referred to as "bulbar scars", are tiny flake scars that appear on some bulbs of applied force. The reason they form is not entirely understood. Of those flakes that do exhibit eraillures, very few have more than one.
ai_text: A lithic flake is a detached fragment generated during lithic reduction when a piece is removed from a core by a detachment blow or applied pressure. The proximal aspect features a striking platform, the surface where the force is delivered, which may be a natural facet of the core or a surface that has been deliberately prepared. The distal end, or termination, describes how the flake separates from the core and can be categorized into several commonly observed styles: feathered, hinged, stepped, and plunging (also known as overshot or outrepassé). Feathered terminations yield a very sharp edge, with the flake thinning gradually as the applied force exits the core. Hinged terminations arise when the force is deflected and rolls away from the core, leaving a rounded distal edge. Stepped terminations occur if the flake breaks during removal, often producing a squared distal end. Plunging terminations involve the force returning toward the core, sometimes removing material from the ventral side. Abrupt terminations encompass hinge, step, and plunging types and may be deliberate in some instances but are more commonly the result of errors, signaling internal core flaws or prior Hertzian cones. Eraillures, or bulbar scars, are small flake scars on the bulbs of applied force, and their origin remains not fully understood. When eraillures are present, they are relatively uncommon, with very few flakes bearing more than one such scar.

human_text: Porcini are sold fresh in markets in summer and autumn in Europe and Russia, and dried or canned at other times of the year, and distributed worldwide to countries where they are not otherwise found. They are eaten and enjoyed raw, sautéed with butter, ground into pasta, in soups, and in many other dishes. In France, they are used in recipes such as cèpes à la Bordelaise, cèpe frits and cèpe aux tomates. Porcini risotto is a traditional Italian autumn dish. Porcini are a feature of many cuisines, including Provençal, and Viennese. In Thailand they are used in soups and consumed blanched in salads. Porcini can also be frozen, either while raw or after cooking in butter. The colour, aroma, and taste of porcini deteriorate noticeably after being frozen for four months. Blanching (or soaking and blanching) as a processing step before freezing can extend the freezer life to 12 months. They are also one of the few species sold commercially as pickled mushrooms.

human_text: Today, most audio file formats and digital audio workstations (DAWs) support PCM formats with samples represented by floating-point numbers. Both the WAV file format and the AIFF file format support floating-point representations. Unlike integers, whose bit pattern is a single series of bits, a floating-point number is instead composed of separate fields whose mathematical relation forms a number. The most common standard is IEEE 754, which is composed of three fields: a sign bit representing whether the number is positive or negative, a mantissa, and an exponent determining a power-of-two factor to scale the mantissa. The mantissa is expressed as a binary fraction in IEEE base-two floating-point formats.
ai_text: Resolution in digital audio is largely determined by the precision of PCM samples, and most audio formats and digital audio workstations encode these samples in floating-point form. WAV and AIFF are containers that support floating-point PCM representations. Floating-point numbers differ from integers in that they are organized as separate fields rather than a single fixed bit pattern. The most widely used standard for such representations is IEEE 754. Under IEEE 754, a number is described by three components: a sign bit, a mantissa, and an exponent. The exponent establishes the magnitude by applying a power-of-two scaling to the mantissa, which is expressed as a binary fraction in base-two floating-point formats.

human_text: The 2005 Base Realignment and Closure Commission preliminary list was released by the United States Department of Defense on May 13, 2005.  It was the fifth Base Realignment and Closure ("BRAC") proposal generated since the process was created in 1988.  It recommended closing 22 major United States military bases and the "realignment" (either enlarging or shrinking) of 33 others. On September 15, 2005,  President George W. Bush approved the BRAC Commission's recommendations, leaving the fate of the bases in question to the United States Congress.  Congress had a maximum of 45 days to reject the proposal by passing a joint resolution of disapproval, or the recommendations automatically enter into effect. Such a resolution (H.J.Res. 65) was introduced to the House of Representatives on September 23, 2005, by Rep. Ray LaHood (R-IL) (no such resolution was introduced in the Senate). The House took up debate of the resolution on October 26, 2005. The resolution failed to pass by a 324–85 margin, thereby enacting the list of recommendations. The Secretary of Defense was required to begin implementing the recommendations by September 15, 2007, and to complete implementation no later than September 15, 2011.

President George W. Bush endorsed the BRAC recommendations on September 15, 2005, with Congress limited to blocking them through a joint resolution of disapproval within 45 days. On September 23, 2005, Representative Ray LaHood introduced H.J.Res. 65 in the House, while no parallel measure appeared in the Senate. The House subsequently debated the resolution on October 26, 2005, and it failed by a vote of 324–85, thereby implementing the BRAC recommendations. The plan's implementation was scheduled to begin by September 15, 2007, and to be completed by September 15, 2011.

human_text: Cooling preserves food by slowing down the growth and reproduction of microorganisms and the action of enzymes that causes the food to rot. The introduction of commercial and domestic refrigerators drastically improved the diets of many in the Western world by allowing food such as fresh fruit, salads and dairy products to be stored safely for longer periods, particularly during warm weather.

The widespread adoption of both domestic and commercial refrigeration significantly improved diets in the Western world by enabling perishable items to be kept for longer periods without compromising safety or quality. Refrigeration facilitates the storage of a variety of foods, including fresh fruit, salads, and dairy products, and helps maintain their texture, flavor, and nutritional value over extended times. The benefits of cooling are particularly pronounced in warm weather, when higher temperatures can accelerate spoilage and microbial growth.

human_text: Pasteurization is a process for preservation of liquid food. It was originally applied to combat the souring of young local wines. Today, the process is mainly applied to dairy products. In this method, milk is heated at about 70 °C (158 °F) for 15–30 seconds to kill the bacteria present in it and cooling it quickly to 10 °C (50 °F) to prevent the remaining bacteria from growing. The milk is then stored in sterilized bottles or pouches in cold places. This method was invented by Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, in 1862.

In the process, milk is heated to approximately 70 °C (158 °F) for 15 to 30 seconds to destroy bacteria, then rapidly cooled to around 10 °C (50 °F) to inhibit remaining microorganisms from multiplying. The treated milk is stored in sterilized bottles or pouches and kept in cold environments to maintain safety and extend shelf life. The technique was introduced by French chemist Louis Pasteur in 1862.

Thai Malays native to the southern region account for roughly three percent. In the northern provinces, hill-tribe communities such as the Hmong and Mien, the Karen, and other smaller hill tribes collectively exceed one percent.

human_text: In official Thai documents, the term "hill tribe" (chao khao) began to appear in the 1960s. This term highlights a "hill and valley" dichotomy that is based on an ancient social relationship existing in most of northern and western Thailand, as well as in Sipsongpanna and northern Vietnam. For the most part the Dai/Tai/Thai occupied the more fertile intermontane basins and valleys, while the less powerful groups lived at the less rich higher elevations. This dichotomy was often accompanied by a master/serf relationship. Vestiges of this dichotomy remain today: for example, 30 percent of ethnic minority children in Thailand cannot read by second grade. The corresponding figure for Bangkok is one percent.
ai_text: The term hill tribe (chao khao) began appearing in official Thai documents in the 1960s. It embodies a historic hill-and-valley dichotomy grounded in long-standing social relations in northern and western Thailand, as well as in adjacent areas such as Sipsongpanna and northern Vietnam. Historically, the Dai, Tai, and Thai groups occupied the more fertile intermontane basins and valleys, while less powerful groups resided in higher elevations. This dichotomy was frequently accompanied by master–serf relationships. Today, vestiges of these patterns persist in education outcomes, with roughly 30 percent of ethnic minority children in Thailand unable to read by the end of the second grade, compared with about 1 percent in Bangkok.

ai_text: Athenae (Pontus) is described by Arrian as an abandoned fortress, while Procopius portrays it as a thriving settlement in his era. In scholarly tradition, Konrad Mannert identifies Athenae with the Odeinus (also rendered Odeinius) named in the Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax, presenting a hypothesized link between the Pontic site and the historical itinerary's geographic nomenclature.

human_text: Athenae or Athenai (Ancient Greek: Ἀθῆναι) was a city and port of ancient Pontus, with a Greek temple of Athena. According to Arrian, it was 180 stadia east of the river Adienus, and 280 stadia west of Apsarus. Procopius writes that the name of the village came from a certain woman named Athenaea (Ancient Greek: Ἀθηναία) in early times who ruled over the land and not because, as some believe, of colonists from Athens settled there. He also adds that the tomb of the woman was still there.
ai_text: Athenae (Pontus) was a city and port in ancient Pontus. It housed a Greek temple dedicated to Athena. Arrian records its location as 180 stadia east of the river Adienus and 280 stadia west of Apsarus. Procopius offers an alternative account of the toponym, deriving the name from a woman named Athenaea who ruled the land rather than from colonists from Athens. He notes that Athenaea's tomb remained at the site.

human_text: USS Edward Rutledge (AP-52/APA-24) was an Edward Rutledge-class troop transport (AP), later re-designated as an attack transport (APA). She was acquired by the U.S. Navy for use in World War II, and was assigned the task of transporting troops to and from battle areas. Operating in dangerous Mediterranean waters on 12 November 1942, she was sunk after being struck by a German submarine’s torpedo at Fedala Bay, Morocco.
ai_text: The USS Edward Rutledge (AP-52), later redesignated APA-24, was an Edward Rutledge-class troop transport (AP) acquired by the United States Navy for World War II use. Its primary role was to transport troops to and from battle areas. On 12 November 1942, during operations in the Mediterranean, the vessel was sunk after being struck by a torpedo from a German submarine in Fedala Bay, Morocco.

human_text: On 12 November she was torpedoed by U-130 commanded by Ernst Kals, who slipped past the escort screen to sink three transports. Edward Rutledge's crew attempted to beach her but all power had been lost; she settled rapidly by the stern and sank with the loss of 15 men.
ai_text: On 12 November 1942, the United States Navy transport USS Edward Rutledge (AP-52) was torpedoed by the German submarine U-130, which was commanded by Ernst Kals. The submarine managed to slip past the convoy’s escort screen and sank three transports in the attack. After losing power, the Edward Rutledge attempted to beach herself, but she ultimately sank by the stern, with fifteen men killed.

human_text: Noted theorist Max Weber suggested that classic feudalism in pre-modern-state Europe was an example of warlordism, as the state regime was unable to "exercise a monopoly on the use of force within its territory" and the monarch relied on the commitment of loyal knights and other nobility to mobilize their private armies in support of the crown for specific military campaigns. As noted French philosopher Alexis de Tocqueville and political scientists such as E. J. Hobsbawm and Theda Skocpol observed in their analyses of the Ancien Régime, the French Revolution and democratization in Europe, that commitment was contingent upon a bargaining process in which the king or queen had to guarantee additional territory, revenue, status or other privileges, meaning that these early European states were weak and the relationship between the crown and feudal lords constituted the form of interdependent warlordism known as cooperative warlord politics.
ai_text: Warlordism, as Max Weber described classic feudalism in pre-modern Europe, emerges when the state fails to monopolize coercive force, leaving political power distributed among competing warlords. In this arrangement, the monarch depended on the loyalty of knights and the nobility to mobilize private armed retinues for campaigns, effectively outsourcing the use of force. The perspectives of Tocqueville, Hobsbawm, and Skocpol hold that commitment from elites and subjects rested on reciprocal bargains, with crowns granting territory, revenue, status, or privileges in exchange for allegiance and service. Consequently, early European states exhibited weak central authority rather than strong centralized sovereignty. The crown–feudal lord relationship is described as interdependent warlordism, or cooperative warlord politics, underscoring mutual dependence between crown and nobles. This framework is relevant to the Ancien Régime, the French Revolution, and broader democratization in Europe, illustrating how shifts in bargaining power influenced state formation and political change.

human_text: Warlordism in Europe is usually connected to various mercenary companies and their chieftains, which often were de facto powerholders in the areas where they resided. Such free companies would arise in a situation when the recognized central power had collapsed, such as in the Great Interregnum in Germany (1254–78), in France during the Hundred Years' War after the Battle of Poitiers, or in the Kingdom of Scotland during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
ai_text: Warlordism in Europe developed in contexts where mercenary companies and their leaders acquired de facto political authority within territories, often serving as local rulers in the absence of a strong central government. These chieftains could command private military forces that controlled towns or districts, effectively governing in place of the monarchy or state institutions. The formation of free companies tended to occur when the legitimate central authority collapsed or weakened, creating a vacuum that such leaders could fill. Prominent historical instances include the Great Interregnum in Germany (1254–1278), the fragmentation of royal power in France during the Hundred Years' War after the Battle of Poitiers, and the Kingdom of Scotland's experience during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
