ai_text: Beach nourishment is a coastal management technique that replenishes eroding shorelines with sand to widen beaches and restore dune systems, thereby reducing erosion and protecting upland areas. The freshly deposited sand can harden over time, potentially hindering sea turtle nest digging and influencing nesting success. At the same time, nourishment can enhance habitat quality and availability for sea turtles, seabirds, and beach vegetation by increasing habitat complexity and vegetation cover. In Florida, to address the risk of turtles being drawn into dredge pumps during nourishment operations, authorities installed a specialized grill on the dredge pipes to prevent entrainment.

human_text: Typical physical measures include dry beach width/height, post-storm sand volume, post-storm damage avoidance assessments and aqueous sand volume.
ai_text: Beach nourishment involves adding sand along a shoreline to widen the dry beach area and raise the beach profile, thereby improving resilience to storms. The success of such projects is assessed by tracking changes in the dry beach width and elevation, as well as the total volume of sand in the nourished zone, including the portion that remains submerged in the nearshore (aqueous sand volume). After storm events, analysts evaluate the remaining sand volume to understand sediment loss and redistribution. They also conduct assessments of damages avoided by the widened beach to determine the extent to which the nourishment mitigates impacts to infrastructure and coastal ecosystems, informing maintenance planning and future management decisions.

human_text: By the Chari River south of Lake Chad the Sao civilisation flourished for over a millennium beginning in the 6th century BC, in territory that later became part of present-day Cameroon and Chad. Their material culture reveals sophisticated bronze, copper, and iron workmanship, including bronze sculptures, terracotta figurines of both humans and animals, coins, funerary urns, domestic utensils, jewelry, decorated pottery, and spears. In the southwest of Cameroon, the Ekoi civilization arose around Lake Ejagham, with origins dating to roughly the 2nd century CE. The Ekoi are particularly noted for the Ikom monoliths and for the development of the Nsibidi writing system.

human_text: After the evolution of Homo sapiens approximately 350,000 to 260,000 years BP in Africa, the continent was mainly populated by groups of hunter-gatherers. These first modern humans left Africa and populated the rest of the globe during the Out of Africa II migration dated to approximately 50,000 years BP, exiting the continent either across Bab-el-Mandeb over the Red Sea, the Strait of Gibraltar in Morocco, or the Isthmus of Suez in Egypt.
ai_text: Homo sapiens originated in Africa between about 350,000 and 260,000 years before present, after which the continent was largely populated by hunter-gatherer communities. Around 50,000 years ago, a later migratory wave—often described as Out of Africa II—led to the spread of modern humans to the rest of the globe. Exits from Africa occurred via three principal routes: Bab-el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea, the Strait of Gibraltar between Africa and Europe, and the Isthmus of Suez in northeastern Egypt.

human_text: It was a common a belief that if a squatter and their friends could—between sunrise and sunset in a single day—build a house on common land, raise the roof over their head and light a fire in the hearth, then they would have the right of undisturbed possession. The belief—sometimes called "keyhole tenure", and which persisted as recently as the early 20th century—was actually a fallacy, but to stop landless peasants unlawfully squatting on commons, the Erection of Cottages Act 1588 (31 Eliz. 1. c. 7) was introduced.
ai_text: Among the historical notions surrounding common land was a widespread but erroneous belief that a squatter could secure undisturbed possession by erecting a house on such land within a single day, from dawn to dusk, a practice popularly known as “keyhole tenure.” Although this belief persisted into the early twentieth century, it is regarded as a fallacy. To deter landless peasants from unlawfully squatting on commons, the Erection of Cottages Act 1588 (31 Eliz. 1. c. 7) was enacted.

human_text: Most end-to-end encryption protocols include some form of endpoint authentication specifically to prevent MITM attacks. For example, one could rely on certification authorities or a web of trust. An alternative technique is to generate cryptographic hashes (fingerprints) based on the communicating users’ public keys or shared secret keys. The parties compare their fingerprints using an outside (out-of-band) communication channel that guarantees integrity and authenticity of communication (but not necessarily secrecy), before starting their conversation. If the fingerprints match, there is, in theory, no man in the middle.
ai_text: End-to-end encryption protocols ensure that only the intended endpoints can access plaintext messages, with endpoint authentication a key mechanism for preventing man-in-the-middle incursions. Common authentication methods include the use of certificates issued by trusted authorities (CAs) or the establishment of a web of trust. An alternative approach is to generate cryptographic fingerprints, or hashes, of the communicating parties’ public keys or of their shared secret keys. These fingerprints are then compared via an out-of-band channel that guarantees integrity and authenticity, though it does not necessarily assure secrecy. The verification takes place before any conversational data is exchanged. When the fingerprints align, a man-in-the-middle attack is, in principle, ruled out.

human_text: In his "On the People's Democratic Dictatorship" published on July 1, 1949, Mao articulated the "leaning to one side" foreign policy directive, in which he framed a world divided between the confrontational Socialist and imperialist camps and that "sitting on the fence will not do, nor is there a third road." Thus, faced with the bleak situation and threats from both within and without, consolidating the communist rule under the Cold War framework of the mid-20th century Mao saw the necessity and benefits in firmly siding with the Soviet Union and joining the socialist camp. He perceived the cooperation within the socialist camp as goodwill and sincere assistance in countries' development in contrast to the Marshall Plan, which Mao considered a pretense of exploitation and the US agenda to exert political influence into the recipient countries. For China, materializing rapid industrialization through economic assistance was one of the primary goals, which rendered the need for Soviet economic and technological assistance the driving force behind the 1950 treaty.
ai_text: Following the Communist victory in China, Mao Zedong announced the “leaning to one side” policy on July 1, 1949, signaling an alignment with the Soviet-led socialist bloc and a rejection of any third way in foreign affairs. In a world increasingly divided between socialist and imperialist camps, Beijing sought to consolidate the Communist regime amid both internal and external threats. China thus firmly aligned with the Soviet Union and joined the socialist camp, presenting such cooperation as evidence of goodwill and a means to secure development assistance, in part contrasted with Western initiatives like the Marshall Plan, which Beijing viewed as exploitative U.S. influence. Central to this approach was China's aim of rapid industrialization, pursued with the aid of Soviet economic and technological support, which in turn helped drive the 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance and deepen bilateral security and economic cooperation within the socialist bloc.

human_text: The Behistun Inscription (also Bisotun, Bisitun or Bisutun; Persian: بیستون, Old Persian: Bagastana, meaning "the place of god") is a multilingual  Achaemenid royal inscription and large rock relief on a cliff at Mount Behistun in the Kermanshah Province of Iran, near the city of Kermanshah in western Iran, established by Darius the Great (r. 522–486 BC). It was important to the decipherment of cuneiform, as it is the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription, written in Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian (a variety of Akkadian).
ai_text: The Behistun Inscription, also known by its variants Bisotun or Bisutun and bearing the Old Persian toponym Bagastana meaning “the place of god,” is a monumental Achaemenid royal inscription accompanied by a large rock relief carved on a cliff at Mount Behistun in western Iran. It is located in Kermanshah Province near the city of Kermanshah. Commissioned by Darius the Great, who ruled from 522 to 486 BCE, the monument serves as a key royal record of his reign. The inscription is especially notable for its crucial role in the decipherment of cuneiform, as it is the longest known trilingual cuneiform text, containing Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian (Akkadian) versions.

human_text: Shima was an autonomous district of Ise Province, noted as a prosperous fishing region, and during the Nara period governors of the district were responsible for providing annual gifts of fish and abalone to the Emperor. human_text: The rough and craggy down-ice (leeward) side is formed by plucking or quarrying, an erosional process initiated when ice melts slightly by pressure and seeps into cracks in the rock. When the water refreezes, the rock becomes attached to the glacier. But as the glacier continues its forward progress it subjects the stone to frost shattering, ripping chunks away from the rock formation. Studies show that the plucking of the lee side is a much more significant erosional process than the abrasion of the stoss side.
ai_text: Roche moutonnée are glacially sculpted bedrock features formed as a glacier moves over the rock, typically presenting a smoother up-glacier face and a rough, craggy down-ice (lee) side. The rugged lee face results from plucking, a quarrying-like process driven by the pressure of the passing ice. Erosion begins when ice melts under pressure and seeps into fractures in the rock; the infiltrating water refreezes, temporarily causing the rock to adhere to the glacier. As the glacier advances, frost shattering then rips chunks away from the rock, reinforcing the irregular lee surface. Studies indicate that lee-side plucking is a much more significant erosional mechanism than stoss-side abrasion.

human_text: Similar to the diagnosis of alveolar echinococcosis and cystic echinococcosis, the diagnosis of polycystic echinococcosis uses imaging techniques, in particular ultrasonography and CT scans, to detect polycystic structures within the person's body. However, imaging is not the preferred method of diagnosis since the method that is currently considered the standard is the isolation of protoscoleces during surgery or after the person's death, and the identification of definitive features of E. oligarthrus and E. vogeli in these isolated protoscoleces. This is the main way that PE is diagnosed, but some current studies show that PCR may identify E. oligarthrus and E. vogeli in people's tissues. The only drawback of using PCR to diagnose polycystic echinococcosis is that there aren't many genetic sequences that can be used for PCR that are specific only E. oligarthrus or E. vogeli.
ai_text: Echinococcosis is a parasitic disease caused by tapeworms of the genus Echinococcus. Diagnostic imaging, including ultrasound and computed tomography, can reveal multichambered cystic lesions characteristic of the infection, but imaging alone is not regarded as the preferred diagnostic method. The gold-standard diagnosis is the isolation of protoscoleces from surgical specimens or postmortem material, which provides definitive confirmation of the infection. In particular, definitive identification of infections caused by Echinococcus oligarthrus or E. vogeli can be achieved through examination of isolated protoscoleces that display species-specific features. Molecular methods, such as PCR, may identify E. oligarthrus and E. vogeli in tissue samples; however, their utility is limited by the relatively small number of species-specific genetic sequences available for these two species.

human_text: The heavy isotope 15N was first discovered by S. M. Naudé in 1929, and soon after heavy isotopes of the neighbouring elements oxygen and carbon were discovered. It presents one of the lowest thermal neutron capture cross-sections of all isotopes. It is frequently used in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to determine the structures of nitrogen-containing molecules, due to its fractional nuclear spin of one-half, which offers advantages for NMR such as narrower line width. 14N, though also theoretically usable, has an integer nuclear spin of one and thus has a quadrupole moment that leads to wider and less useful spectra. 15N NMR nevertheless has complications not encountered in the more common 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy. The low natural abundance of 15N (0.36%) significantly reduces sensitivity, a problem which is only exacerbated by its low gyromagnetic ratio, (only 10.14% that of 1H). As a result, the signal-to-noise ratio for 1H is about 300 times as much as that for 15N at the same magnetic field strength. This may be somewhat alleviated by isotopic enrichment of 15N by chemical exchange or fractional distillation. 15N-enriched compounds have the advantage that under standard conditions, they do not undergo chemical exchange of their nitrogen atoms with atmospheric nitrogen, unlike compounds with labelled hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen isotopes that must be kept away from the atmosphere. The 15N:14N ratio is commonly used in stable isotope analysis in the fields of geochemistry, hydrology, paleoclimatology and paleoceanography, where it is called δ15N.

It possesses a notably low thermal neutron capture cross-section among isotopes. The isotope is widely used in NMR spectroscopy to determine the structures of nitrogen-containing molecules because its nuclear spin of 1/2 allows relatively narrow resonance lines; by contrast, the predominant 14N has spin 1 and a quadrupole moment that broadens spectra. Consequently, 15N NMR presents certain complications not encountered in 1H or 13C NMR. Unlike labeled hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen compounds, 15N-enriched materials generally do not exchange with atmospheric N2 under standard conditions. The 15N to 14N ratio, referred to as δ15N, is used in stable isotope analyses across geochemistry, hydrology, paleoclimatology, and paleoceanography.

human_text: HDCAM is a high-definition video digital recording videocassette version of Digital Betacam introduced in 1997 that uses an 8-bit discrete cosine transform (DCT) compressed 3:1:1 recording, in 1080i-compatible down-sampled resolution of 1440 × 1080, and adding 24p and 23.976 progressive segmented frame (PsF) modes to later models. The HDCAM codec uses rectangular pixels and as such the recorded 1440 × 1080 content is upsampled to 1920 × 1080 on playback. The recorded video bit rate is 144 Mbit/s. Audio is also similar, with four channels of AES3 20-bit, 48 kHz digital audio. Like Betacam, HDCAM tapes were produced in small and large cassette sizes; the small cassette uses the same form factor as the original Betamax. The main competitor to HDCAM was the DVCPRO HD format offered by Panasonic, which uses a similar compression scheme and bit rates ranging from 40 to 100 Mbit/s depending on frame rate.
ai_text: HDCAM is a high-definition digital videocassette format developed as a high-definition recording variant of Digital Betacam, introduced in 1997. It uses an 8-bit DCT encoding with 3:1:1 chroma subsampling for recording. The format records 1440×1080 content, which is down-sampled to be compatible with 1080i systems; later generations added support for 24p and 23.976 PsF. The codec employs rectangular pixels, and playback upscales 1440×1080 material to 1920×1080. The video bitrate is approximately 144 Mbps. Audio is carried as four AES3 digital channels at 20-bit depth and 48 kHz. Tapes are available in small and large cassette sizes, with the small cartridge sharing the same form factor as the original Betamax. The principal competitor is Panasonic's DVCPRO HD, which uses a similar compression and offers a bitrate ranging roughly from 40 to 100 Mbps depending on frame rate.

Clothing crafted from fur and hides of hunted animals facilitated expansion into colder regions. Additionally, Homo sapiens began migrating out of Africa around 200,000 years ago, with initial movements into Eurasia.

Javanese script was actively used by the Javanese people for writing day-to-day and literary texts from at least the mid-16th century CE until the mid-20th century CE, before it was gradually supplanted by the Latin alphabet. human_text: Intergovernmental organizations are provided with privileges and immunities that are intended to ensure their independent and effective functioning. The organizations are thereby immune from the jurisdiction of national courts. human_text: In measure and probability theory in mathematics, a convex measure is a probability measure that — loosely put — does not assign more mass to any intermediate set "between" two measurable sets A and B than it does to A or B individually.  There are multiple ways in which the comparison between the probabilities of A and B and the intermediate set can be made, leading to multiple definitions of convexity, such as log-concavity, harmonic convexity, and so on.  The mathematician Christer Borell was a pioneer of the detailed study of convex measures on locally convex spaces in the 1970s.

Different schemes for comparing the probabilities of A, B, and their intermediate sets give rise to several definitions of convexity, including concepts such as log-concavity and harmonic convexity. Christer Borell is recognized as a pioneer in the detailed study of convex measures on locally convex spaces, beginning in the 1970s.

human_text: In personnel economics, some researchers take the view that seniority pay is employed by firms as a solution to the problem of shirking. Since firms cannot always monitor the effort of their employees, they need to introduce an incentive for their employees to keep up the work. One way firms can accomplish this is through delayed compensation, in which employees are paid below the value of what they are producing in the first years at a firm, and paid above the value of their production in later years. The continuous rising of the wage based on seniority at the firm ensures that shirking, which can lead to dismissal, becomes much more costly for employees due to the loss of the high wages they can expect when staying at a firm for a long time.

Firms may employ delayed compensation schemes in which initial pay falls short of the discounted value of early output, while later earnings exceed it, thereby encouraging sustained effort. As tenure increases, wages rise progressively, producing a continuous upward trajectory with time on the job. The prospect of dismissal and the loss of higher, tenure‑linked future wages heightens the cost of shirking, reinforcing effort and aligning employees’ incentives with long‑run employment.

human_text: The principal Swazi social unit is the homestead, a traditional beehive hut thatched with dry grass. In a polygamous homestead, each wife has her own hut and yard surrounded by reed fences. There are three structures for sleeping, cooking, and storage (brewing beer). Larger homesteads also have structures used as bachelors' quarters and guest accommodation. Central to the traditional homestead is the cattle byre, a circular area enclosed by large logs, interspersed with branches. The cattle byre has ritual as well as practical significance as a store of wealth and symbol of prestige. It contains sealed grain pits. Facing the cattle byre is the great hut which is occupied by the mother of the headman. The headman is central to all homestead affairs, and he is often polygamous. He leads through example and advises his wives on all social affairs of the home, as well as seeing to the well-being of the family. He also spends time socialising with the young boys, who are often his sons or close relatives, advising them on the expectations of growing up and manhood.

human_text: The Sixteen Kingdoms (simplified Chinese: 十六国; traditional Chinese: 十六國; pinyin: Shíliù Guó), less commonly the Sixteen States, was a chaotic period in Chinese history from AD 304 to 439 when northern China fragmented into a series of short-lived dynastic states. Most of these regimes were created by groups such as the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Jie, and Qiang, who had moved into northern and western China over earlier centuries and rose in rebellion against the Western Jin dynasty in the early fourth century. Some states were founded by the Han as well. Regardless of their rulers' background, every state adopted dynastic institutions in the Han tradition and styled itself as a legitimate monarchy. These states often fought one another and also contended with the Eastern Jin dynasty, which governed the south after the collapse of Western Jin in 317. The era ended in 439, when Northern Wei, founded by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei, reunified the north. The Eastern Jin dynasty had already collapsed in 420 and been replaced by the Liu Song dynasty, the first of the Southern Dynasties. After the consolidation of the north, Chinese history entered the period known as the Northern and Southern Dynasties.

Regardless of origins, all of the states adopted Han dynasty–style constitutional and administrative forms and claimed legitimate monarchy. In the south, the Eastern Jin collapsed in 420, giving way to Liu Song, the first of the Southern Dynasties. The reunification of the north thus ushered in the broader Northern and Southern Dynasties era.

human_text: Citta-saṃtāna (Sanskrit), literally "the stream of mind", is the continuum, succession, or flow of succeeding moments of mind or awareness. Similarly, the mindstream is the ongoing flow of conscious experience, even though each individual moment of consciousness ceases as the next arises. It provides a continuity of mentation in the absence of a permanently abiding "self" (ātman), which Buddhism denies. The mindstream provides a continuity from one life to another, akin to the flame of a candle which may be passed from one candle to another: William Waldron writes that "Indian Buddhists see the 'evolution' of mind i[n] terms of the continuity of individual mind-streams from one lifetime to the next, with karma as the basic causal mechanism whereby transformations are transmitted from one life to the next."

The mindstream denotes the ongoing flow of conscious experience and provides continuity of mentation without a permanently abiding self (ātman), a concept Buddhist doctrine denies. This continuity is conceived as persisting from one life to another, often illustrated by the analogy of a candle flame passed from one candle to another. Indian Buddhist thought views the evolution of mind as the persistence of individual mind-streams across lifetimes, with karma functioning as the primary causal mechanism that transmits transformations from one life to the next.

Compared with base-load plants, gas turbine units generally incur higher operating costs. These facilities are often comparatively compact and can be operated unmanned or remotely. human_text: The Wallemiomycetes are a class of fungi in the division Basidiomycota. It consists of the single order Wallemiales, containing the single family Wallemiaceae, which in turn contains the single genus Wallemia. The phylogenetic origin of the lineage was placed to various parts of Basidiomycota, but according to the analysis of a larger dataset it is a sister group of Agaricomycotina. The genus contains species of xerophilic molds that are found worldwide. The seven described species (W. sebi, W. ichthyophaga, W. muriae, W. mellicola, W. canadensis, W. tropicalis, and W. hederae) are distinguished by conidial size, xerotolerance, halotolerance, chaotolerance, growth temperature regimes, extracellular enzyme activity profiles, and secondary metabolite patterns. They are typically isolated from low-moisture foods (such as cakes, bread, sugar, peanuts, dried fish), indoor air dust, salterns and soil. W. sebi is thought to be one of the causes of the hypersensitivity pneumonitis known as the farmer's lung disease, but since the other species were recognised and separated from W. sebi only recently, their role in the disease cannot be excluded.

human_text: Tolerance to low water activity is generally much more frequent among ascomycetous than basidomycetous fungi, and xerotolerant fungi are also able to grow in regular growth media with normal water activity (unlike, for example, halophilic Archaea). human_text: If people who live agreeably are Epicureans, none are more truly Epicurean than the righteous and godly.  And if it is names that bother us, no one better deserves the name of Epicurean than the revered founder and head of the Christian philosophy Christ, for in Greek epikouros means "helper".  He alone, when the law of Nature was all but blotted out by sins, when the law of Moses incited to lists rather than cured them, when Satan ruled in the world unchallenged, brought timely aid to perishing humanity.  Completely mistaken, therefore, are those who talk in their foolish fashion about Christ's having been sad and gloomy in character and calling upon us to follow a dismal mode of life.  On the contrary, he alone shows the most enjoyable life of all and the one most full of true pleasure.
ai_text: Within Renaissance humanism, some thinkers linked the pursuit of a harmonious, agreeable life with Epicureanism, arguing that the truly righteous and devout embody Epicurean ideals. In this framework, epikouros, meaning “helper,” was invoked to portray Christ as the supreme Epicurean in name, and as the founder or head of Christian philosophy. Proponents maintained that Christ arrived as timely aid when nature’s law seemed obscured by sin, when the Mosaic Law provoked rather than healed, and when Satan purportedly ruled unchecked. They rejected claims that Christ was sad or that life should be gloomy, contending instead that Christ alone demonstrates the most enjoyable life and true pleasure.

human_text: The use of tautologies, however, is usually unintentional. For example, the phrases "mental telepathy", "planned conspiracies", and "small dwarfs" imply that there are such things as physical telepathy, spontaneous conspiracies, and giant dwarfs, which are oxymorons.
ai_text: In linguistics, tautologies in ordinary language are typically unintentional, arising when two terms with overlapping meanings are paired. Common illustrations include phrases that blend mental processes with telepathic ability, descriptions of conspiracies as if they were planned, and references to dwarfs described as small. These formulations imply the existence of contrary qualities, such as a physical form of telepathy, conspiracies that occur spontaneously, or dwarfs of considerable size. Consequently, such expressions are regarded as oxymorons, defined by the juxtaposition of contradictory terms.

human_text: Intentional repetition of meaning intends to amplify or emphasize a particular, usually significant fact about what is being discussed. For example, a gift is, by definition, free of charge; using the phrase "free gift" might emphasize that there are no hidden conditions or fine print (such as the expectation of money or reciprocation) or that the gift is being given by volition.
ai_text: Tautology in language is the intentional repetition of meaning to amplify or emphasize a significant fact about the topic under discussion. It is used to underscore or reinforce a point in communication. A typical example is the phrase “free gift,” which signals that there are no hidden conditions or fine print, or that the gift is extended voluntarily. A related instance is the statement that “a gift is, by definition, free of charge,” which shows tautology through the inherent sense of the terms involved.

human_text: Andrew Marvell died suddenly in 1678, while attending a popular meeting of his old constituents at Hull. His health had been remarkably good; and some people theorised of his poisoning by his political or clerical enemies. This is unproven. Marvell was buried in the church of St Giles in the Fields in central London. His monument, erected by a very grateful constituency, bears the following inscription:Near this place lyeth the body of Andrew Marvell, Esq., a man so endowed by Nature, so improved by Education, Study, and Travel, so consummated by Experience, that, joining the peculiar graces of Wit and Learning, with a singular penetration and strength of judgment; and exercising all these in the whole course of his life, with an unutterable steadiness in the ways of Virtue, he became the ornament and example of his age, beloved by good men, feared by bad, admired by all, though imitated by few; and scarce paralleled by any. But a Tombstone can neither contain his character, nor is Marble necessary to transmit it to posterity; it is engraved in the minds of this generation, and will be always legible in his inimitable writings, nevertheless. He having served twenty years successfully in Parliament, and that with such Wisdom, Dexterity, and Courage, as becomes a true Patriot, the town of Kingston-upon-Hull, from whence he was deputed to that Assembly, lamenting in his death the public loss, have erected this Monument of their Grief and their Gratitude, 1688.
ai_text: Andrew Marvell died suddenly in 1678 while attending a popular meeting of his old Hull constituents. Although his health had been notably good, allegations of poisoning by political or clerical enemies circulated but remain unproven. He was buried in the church of St Giles in the Fields in central London. Kingston-upon-Hull erected a monument bearing a long inscription that praises him as endowed by Nature, refined by Education, Study, and Travel, and perfected by Experience. The inscription credits him with combining wit and learning with penetrating and strong judgment, and with steadiness in the ways of Virtue. He is depicted as an ornament and example of his age, beloved by good, feared by bad, admired by all, though imitated by few, scarcely paralleled by any. A tombstone is said to be insufficient to contain his character, which, the inscription notes, is engraved in the minds of his generation and in his writings. He served twenty years in Parliament with Wisdom, Dexterity, and Courage, as a true Patriot, well-regarded by Kingston-upon-Hull. The town lamented his death and in 1688 erected the monument as an expression of their grief and gratitude.

The name also reverses the syllables of Airvault, his family's home town in the Poitou region.

ai_text: Ramparts encompass a range of defensive earthworks, from simple dump ramparts consisting of earth-and-stone mounds to more elaborate earth-and-timber barriers. Some ramparts are reinforced by stone revetments to improve durability against attack or weathering. In Central Europe, the Pfostenschlitzmauer, or post-slot wall, exemplifies a regional variant that combines earth, stone, and wooden posts to create a sturdy barrier. Vitrified ramparts are stone ramparts that have been fired to increase their strength, a technique intended to bind the materials and enhance defensive performance.

human_text: The expedition's failure weakened the Umayyad state. As historian Bernard Lewis commented, "Its failure brought a grave moment for Umayyad power. The financial strain of equipping and maintaining the expedition caused an aggravation of the fiscal and financial oppression which had already aroused such dangerous opposition. The destruction of the fleet and army of Syria at the sea walls of Constantinople deprived the regime of the chief material basis of its power". The blow to the Caliphate's might was severe, and although the land army did not suffer losses in the same degree as the fleet, Umar is recorded as contemplating withdrawing from the recent conquests of Hispania and Transoxiana, as well as a complete evacuation of Cilicia and other Byzantine territories that the Arabs had seized over the previous years. Although his advisors dissuaded him from such drastic actions, most Arab garrisons were withdrawn from the Byzantine frontier districts they had occupied in the lead-up to the siege. In Cilicia, only Mopsuestia remained in Arab hands as a defensive bulwark to protect Antioch. The Byzantines even recovered some territory in western Armenia for a time. In 719, the Byzantine fleet raided the Syrian coast and burned down the port of Laodicea and, in 720 or 721, the Byzantines attacked and sacked Tinnis in Egypt. Leo also restored control over Sicily, where news of the Arab siege of Constantinople and expectations of the city's fall had prompted the local governor to declare an emperor of his own, Basil Onomagoulos. It was during this time, however, that effective Byzantine control over Sardinia and Corsica ceased.

As a result, most Arab garrisons were withdrawn from the Byzantine frontier districts, with only Mopsuestia in Cilicia remaining as a defensive bulwark for Antioch. human_text: Although an outcome may be a Pareto improvement, this does not imply that the outcome is equitable. It is possible that inequality persists even after a Pareto improvement. Despite the fact that it is frequently used in conjunction with the idea of Pareto optimality, the term "efficiency" refers to the process of increasing societal productivity. It is possible for a society to have Pareto efficiency while also have high levels of inequality. Consider the following scenario: there is a pie and three persons; the most equitable way would be to divide the pie into three equal portions. However, if the pie is divided in half and shared between two people, it is considered Pareto efficient –  meaning that the third person does not lose out (despite the fact that he does not receive a piece of the pie). When making judgments, it is critical to consider a variety of aspects, including social efficiency, overall welfare, and issues such as diminishing marginal value.
ai_text: Pareto efficiency, also known as Pareto optimality, describes an allocation in which no reallocation can make someone better off without making someone else worse off. A Pareto improvement can occur without achieving equity, meaning inequality can persist even after such gains. The concept is concerned with the efficiency of the allocation process and is about productive performance rather than fairness. Consequently, a society may be Pareto efficient even when inequality is substantial. For example, in a simple division of a pie among three individuals, the fairest outcome would be equal shares for all, yet allocating the entire pie to two people while leaving the third with nothing can still be Pareto efficient because the third party is not worse off. Evaluations of Pareto efficiency should consider multiple dimensions, including social efficiency, overall welfare, and the diminishing marginal value of additional resources.

ai_text: Provincial cities in Taiwan were historically administered under the provincial governments of the Republic of China. In 1998, the provincial system underwent a reform that effectively downgraded the provinces to non-self-governing bodies with diminished authority. A subsequent reform in 2018 led to the formal abolition of all provincial governmental organs. Today, provincial cities, together with counties, function as the de facto principal subnational divisions under the direction of the central government of the Republic of China.

human_text: In the early 1900s, Bethpage (then called Central Park) was home to a small village of early Scandinavian immigrants, whose area was north of Cherry Avenue, east of Stewart Avenue, and west of today's Seaford Oyster Bay Expressway. A Scandinavian-American Club of North Central Park formed in 1924, called Central Park North Civic Association, whose social activities and project fundraising helped improve roads, street lighting, water service, and postal service. After officially disbanding in 1959, the clubhouse, located on Stewart Avenue, became Saint Isidoro's Greek Orthodox Church.
ai_text: Bethpage, New York, was historically referred to as Central Park in the early 20th century and served as a small enclave for Scandinavian immigrants. The settlement lay north of Cherry Avenue, east of Stewart Avenue, and west of today’s Seaford Oyster Bay Expressway. In 1924, the Scandinavian-American Club of North Central Park was formed, also known as the Central Park North Civic Association. Through its social activities and fundraising, the organization contributed to improvements in local infrastructure, including roads, street lighting, water service, and postal service. The group disbanded in 1959, after which the clubhouse on Stewart Avenue was repurposed as Saint Isidoro’s Greek Orthodox Church.

human_text: Between 1851 and 1854, the LIRR initiated a stop within present-day Bethpage at a station then called Jerusalem Station, and on January 29, 1857, a local post office opened, also named Jerusalem Station. LIRR schedules listed the station also as simply Jerusalem. Residents succeeded in changing the name of the post office to Central Park, effective March 1, 1867 (respelled as Centralpark from 1895 to 1899). The Central Park Fire Company was organized in April 1910, and incorporated in May 1911. In May 1923 the Central Park Water District was created.
ai_text: In the area now known as Bethpage, the Long Island Rail Road established a stop sometime between 1851 and 1854, originally called Jerusalem Station. A local post office began operation on January 29, 1857 under the Jerusalem Station name, and LIRR timetables continued to list the stop as Jerusalem. In 1867, residents renamed the post office Central Park, with the change taking effect on March 1 of that year, and the spelling Centralpark appeared in use from 1895 to 1899. The Central Park Fire Company was organized in April 1910 and incorporated in May 1911, and the Central Park Water District was created in May 1923.

human_text: During the 1982 World Cup in Spain, Austria and West Germany met again, in the last match of the group stage. Because the other two teams in the group had played their last match the previous day, both teams knew that a West German win by one goal would see both through, while all other results would eliminate one team or the other. After ten minutes of furious attack, Horst Hrubesch scored for West Germany, and the two teams mainly kicked the ball around for 80 minutes with few attempts to attack. The match became known as the "non-aggression pact of Gijón". Algeria had also won two matches, including a shocking surprise over West Germany in the opener, but among the three teams that had won two matches, was eliminated based on goal difference, having conceded two late goals in their 3–2 win over Chile. This match caused outrage between supporters of multiple national teams; as a result, all future tournaments would see the last group matches played simultaneously. Austria and Northern Ireland were eliminated by losing to France in the second round group stage of three teams.
ai_text: During the 1982 FIFA World Cup in Spain, the Austria national football team contested its final group match against West Germany, a game that became infamous as the non-aggression pact of Gijón: with both sides already able to advance only if West Germany won by a single goal, the match concluded with a 1–0 victory for West Germany, Horst Hrubesch scoring after about ten minutes and the remainder of the game largely uneventful. Algeria, despite recording two wins including a shock victory over West Germany, were eliminated on goal difference after conceding late goals in their 3–2 win over Chile. The controversy surrounding the match provoked widespread outrage and prompted changes in future tournaments, with last-group matches subsequently scheduled to be played simultaneously. In the second group stage, Austria and Northern Ireland were eliminated by France in a three-team group.

human_text: On 5 December 1809, Harlequin, still under Anstruther's command, left Plymouth Sound with a convoy of 22 vessels that she was escorting through the English Channel. On the evening of 7 December, she suddenly struck the shore. Her crew chopped away her masts, fired distress guns, and burnt blue lights. Still, six other vessels in the convoy also ran ashore. Apparently, in the darkness, the vessels had mistakenly believed they had passed Beachy Head and so prematurely changed course, with the result that they ran ashore west of Seaford. Two men of Harlequin's crew drowned. Apparently the warning signals saved the 16 other vessels in the convoy.
ai_text: Harlequin, a hired armed ship under Captain Anstruther, departed Plymouth Sound on 5 December 1809 with a convoy of twenty-two vessels bound for the English Channel. On the evening of 7 December she struck the shore west of Seaford after darkness led to a miscalculation of position; the crew cut away the masts, fired distress guns, and burned blue lights to attract aid. Six other ships in the convoy also ran ashore. The cause was attributed to the vessels' erroneous belief in having passed Beachy Head, prompting an premature course change to the west of Seaford. Two members of Harlequin’s crew drowned in the wreck. The warning signals issued by Harlequin and the other ships enabled the remaining sixteen vessels in the convoy to reach safety.

human_text: World War II was described by the company as being the blackest days of its history. In 1938 the Mita and Tamagawa plants were placed under military control, with direct supervision by military officers. In 1939, Nippon Electric established a research laboratory in the Tamagawa plant. It became the first Japanese company to successfully test microwave multiplex communications. On 22 December 1941, the enemy property control law was passed. NEC shares owned by International Standard Electric Corporation (ISE), an ITT subsidiary, and Western Electric affiliate were seized. Capital and technical relations were abruptly severed. The "Munitions Company Law" was passed in October 1943, placing overall control of NEC plants under military jurisdiction. The Ueno plant was leveled by the military attack in March 1945. Fire bombings in April and May heavily damaged the Tamagawa Plant, reducing its capacity by forty percent. The Okayama Plant was totally destroyed by a bombing attack in June of the same year. At the end of the war, NEC's production had been substantially reduced by damage to its facilities, and by material and personnel shortages.

The enactment of the Enemy Property Control Law on December 22, 1941 led to NEC’s shares, then held by ISE (an ITT subsidiary) and a Western Electric affiliate, being seized, terminating its capital and technical relationships. In October 1943 the Munitions Company Law was enacted, placing NEC’s plants under direct military jurisdiction. The war exerted continuing pressure on production, with the Ueno plant leveled by a military attack in March 1945, and the Tamagawa plant heavily damaged by firebombing in April–May, reducing its capacity by about 40 percent; the Okayama plant was completely destroyed in June 1945. By the end of World War II, NEC’s production had been substantially diminished due to damaged facilities, material shortages, and a lack of skilled personnel.

human_text: Early versions of the unity of science thesis can be found in ancient Greek philosophers such as Aristotle, and in the later history of Western philosophy. For example, in the first half of the 20th century the thesis was associated with the unity of science movement led by Otto Neurath, and in the second half of the century the thesis was advocated by Ludwig von Bertalanffy in "General System Theory: A New Approach to Unity of Science" (1951) and by Paul Oppenheim and Hilary Putnam in "Unity of Science as a Working Hypothesis" (1958). It has been opposed by, for example, Jerry Fodor in "Special Sciences (Or: The Disunity of Science as a Working Hypothesis)" (1974), by Paul Feyerabend in Against Method (1975) and later works, by John Dupré in "The Disunity of Science" (1983) and The Disorder of Things: Metaphysical Foundations of the Disunity of Science (1993), by Nancy Cartwright in The Dappled World: A Study of the Boundaries of Science (1999) and other works, and by Evelyn Fox Keller in Making Sense of Life: Explaining Biological Development with Models, Metaphors, and Machines (2002) and other works.
ai_text: The unity of science is a philosophical thesis concerning the coherence and potential reducibility or unification of the sciences within a single overarching framework, a notion with roots in ancient Greek philosophy, particularly Aristotle, and in the Western intellectual tradition. In the early 20th century it gained prominence as part of a broader unity of science movement led by Otto Neurath. In the latter half of the century, its advocates included Ludwig von Bertalanffy with General System Theory (1951) and Paul Oppenheim and Hilary Putnam, who framed the unity of science as a working hypothesis in 1958. The position has faced several significant critiques, notably from Jerry Fodor in his 1974 discussion of the disunity of the special sciences and from Paul Feyerabend in Against Method (1975) and subsequent writings. Later critics have included John Dupré with The Disunity of Science (1983) and The Disorder of Things (1993), Nancy Cartwright with The Dappled World (1999), and Evelyn Fox Keller with Making Sense of Life (2002), among others.

human_text: Jean Piaget suggested, in his 1918 book Recherche and later works, that the unity of science can be considered in terms of a circle of the sciences, where logic is the foundation for mathematics, which is the foundation for mechanics and physics, and physics is the foundation for chemistry, which is the foundation for biology, which is the foundation for sociology, the moral sciences, psychology, and the theory of knowledge, and the theory of knowledge forms a basis for logic, completing the circle, without implying that any science could be reduced to any other. More recently, many complex systems are considered to be transdisciplinary objects of study. Such systems can be modeled as having emergent properties at different levels of organization, which do not neatly correspond to separate disciplines such as physics or biology, and which cannot be adequately modeled using a philosophy of extreme reductionism ("everything comes from the bottom", which does not fully account for emergent properties) or extreme holism ("everything comes from the top", which does not fully account for systems' components and interactions).
ai_text: In the context of the unity of science, Jean Piaget proposed in 1918 (in Recherche) a circular arrangement of the sciences in which foundational relationships link disciplines to one another. He outlined a chain in which logic grounds mathematics, mathematics underpins mechanics and physics, physics thereby supports chemistry, chemistry underpins biology, and biology furnishes the basis for sociology, the moral sciences, psychology, and the theory of knowledge. The theory of knowledge itself serves as a foundation for logic, completing the circle, while explicitly not implying that any science can be reduced to another. The position rejects the notion of reductionism among the sciences. In more recent consideration, many complex systems are treated as transdisciplinary objects of study, notable for emergent properties that appear across multiple levels of organization and do not align neatly with isolated domains such as physics or biology. Such emergent features resist adequate description by extreme reductionism (bottom-up) or extreme holism (top-down).

human_text: In previous generations, some artists made very successful careers of presenting revivals or reworkings of once-popular tunes, even out of doing contemporary cover versions of current hits. Since the 1950s, musicians now play what they call "cover versions" (the reworking, updating, or interpretation) of songs as a tribute to the original performer or group. Using familiar material (such as evergreen hits, standard tunes or classic recordings) is an important method of learning music styles. Until the mid-1960s most albums, or long playing records, contained a large number of evergreens or standards to present a fuller range of the artist's abilities and style. (See, for example, Please Please Me.) Artists might also perform interpretations ("covers") of a favorite artist's hit tunes for the simple pleasure of playing a familiar song or collection of tunes.
ai_text: Cover songs are new performances or recordings of previously released songs by artists other than the original performer. In the early days of popular music, artists often built careers through revivals or reworkings of well-known tunes, including contemporary covers of current hits. From the 1950s onward, the term cover version came to signify reworking, updating, or interpreting songs, frequently as tributes to the original performer or group. Relying on familiar material—evergreen hits, standards, and classic recordings—has long been an important approach for learning musical styles. Through the mid-1960s, many albums included a substantial number of evergreen or standard tracks to showcase an artist’s range; an example is the Beatles’ Please Please Me, which featured several covers alongside original songs. Beyond educational or career-building purposes, covers are also performed for the simple pleasure of playing familiar tunes or collections of familiar songs.

ai_text: Cover songs intersect with licensing and performance rights. Generally, a composer cannot block a new recorded version of a song from being released through a mechanical license, which ensures that the song can be mechanically reproduced by others; however, the creator or publisher may retain the prerogative to decide who may issue the first commercially released recording of the work. An illustrative instance is Bob Dylan, who declined to grant his record company permission to release a live performance of "Mr. Tambourine Man." Despite control over the initial recording, pre-release cover versions of songs can still appear, as performers may record and circulate covers before an official first release.

human_text: State policy has influenced the funding of public works and science for thousands of years, dating at least from the time of the Mohists, who inspired the study of logic  during the period of the Hundred Schools of Thought, and the study of defensive fortifications during the Warring States period in China. General levies of labor and grain were collected to fund great public works in China, including the accumulation of grain for distribution in times of famine, for the building of levees to control flooding by the great rivers of China, for the building of canals and locks to connect rivers of China, some of which flowed in opposite directions to each other, and for  the building of bridges across these rivers. These projects required a civil service, the scholars, some of whom demonstrated great mastery of hydraulics.
ai_text: The history of science policy traces state involvement in funding public works and scientific activity back to ancient times, notably in China where the Mohist school influenced early debates about governance of knowledge. The Mohists fostered the study of logic during the era of the Hundred Schools of Thought, and their thinking also informed approaches to defensive fortifications during the Warring States period. Over successive eras, general levies of labor and grain financed major public works, including famine-relief provisioning, flood-control levees, canals and locks linking rivers that sometimes flowed in opposite directions, and the construction of bridges. The execution of these projects depended on a civil service of scholars who administered and applied technical knowledge. Some of these scholars demonstrated considerable mastery of hydraulics, applying practical water-management techniques to large-scale infrastructure.

human_text: Self-funding and independent wealth were also crucial funding sources for scientists, from the Renaissance at least until the late 19th century.  Many scientists derived income from tangential but related activities: Galileo sold instruments; Kepler published horoscopes; Robert Hooke designed buildings and built watches; and most anatomists and natural historians practiced or taught medicine. Those with independent means were sometimes known as gentlemen scientists.
ai_text: In the history of science policy, self-funding and independent wealth provided crucial support for scientists from the Renaissance through the late nineteenth century. Engagement in science frequently yielded income through related pursuits rather than through scholarly work alone; for example, Galileo sold scientific instruments, Kepler published astrological predictions, Robert Hooke designed buildings and built watches, and anatomists and natural historians practiced medicine or taught it. Those with independent means were commonly described as gentlemen scientists, a label reflecting the social status and economic basis of early scientific enterprise.

human_text: The Kuy language belongs to the Austroasiatic language family, within which several more closely related languages, including Bru, Ta-Oi, and Kuy, among others, make up the Katuic subgroup. In many register-tone languages, low tones may cause a downstep in following high or mid tones; the effect is such that even while the low tones remain at the lower end of the speaker's vocal range (which is itself descending due to downdrift), the high tones drop incrementally like steps in a stairway or terraced rice fields, until finally the tones merge and the system has to be reset. ai_text: Tone in linguistics examines how pitch contrasts function across languages and how tonal systems interact with one another, similar to other phonemic layers such as consonants and vowels. In numerous register-tone languages, a low tone can trigger a downstep in following high or mid tones, lowering their phonetic realization relative to preceding tones. As a consequence, the lower tones occupy the lower end of the vocal range, which itself tends to shift downward through downdrift, causing high tones to drop incrementally across a sequence. The resulting pitch pattern appears as a stair-step or terraced contour, with successive high tones lowering in height. Over time, the interacting tones may merge, erasing contrast until a reset restores distinct tonal values. This phenomenon is referred to as tone terracing.

human_text: Another difference between tonal languages is whether the tones apply independently to each syllable or to the word as a whole. In Cantonese, Thai, and Kru languages, each syllable may have a tone, whereas in Shanghainese, Swedish, Norwegian and many Bantu languages, the contour of each tone operates at the word level. That is, a trisyllabic word in a three-tone syllable-tone language has many more tonal possibilities (3 × 3 × 3 = 27) than a monosyllabic word (3), but there is no such difference in a word-tone language. For example, Shanghainese has two contrastive (phonemic) tones no matter how many syllables are in a word. Many languages described as having pitch accent are word-tone languages.
ai_text: Tone in linguistics refers to systems that use pitch variation to distinguish meaning, either on the level of individual syllables or across whole words. In syllable-tone languages, each syllable may bear its own tone; languages such as Cantonese, Thai, and Kru illustrate this pattern, where a syllable can carry a tone independent of surrounding units. By contrast, word-tone languages organize tone contours at the word level, so the pitch configuration spans multiple syllables rather than being fixed to a single syllable; Shanghainese, Swedish, Norwegian, and many Bantu languages are described as exhibiting word-level tonal contours. In syllable-tone systems with three distinct tones, the number of possible tonal realizations grows multiplicatively with syllable count: a three-syllable word can realize 27 tonal shapes, while a monosyllable has just three. Conversely, in word-tone systems the tonal inventory does not multiply with added syllables; for example, Shanghainese maintains two contrastive tones regardless of word length. Additionally, many languages commonly labeled as having pitch accent are considered to be word-tone languages.

In the first two decades of the 15th century this arrangement was copied in northern Europe where, by the late 1430s, some ships were built with carvel hulls. The result of this merging of traditions was the full-rigged ship, a carvel hull with a sternpost-hung pintle-and-gudgeon rudder and three masts: the foremast and mainmast setting square sails and the mizzen a lateen sail. Alongside this type of vessel, the caravel was used. This type was also carvel built with a sternpost-hung rudder but could be completely lateen rigged or have some square sails.

human_text: Exciting new developments in biotechnology are now revolutionizing biology and biomedical research. Examples of these techniques are high-throughput sequencing, high-throughput quantitative PCR, intra-cellular imaging, in-situ hybridization of gene expression, three-dimensional imaging techniques like Light Sheet Fluorescence Microscopy, and Optical Projection (micro)-Computer Tomography. Given the massive amounts of complicated data that is generated by these techniques, their meaningful interpretation, and even their storage, form major challenges calling for new approaches. Going beyond current bioinformatics approaches, computational biology needs to develop new methods to discover meaningful patterns in these large data sets. Model-based reconstruction of gene networks can be used to organize the gene expression data in a systematic way and to guide future data collection. A major challenge here is to understand how gene regulation is controlling fundamental biological processes like biomineralization and embryogenesis. The sub-processes like gene regulation, organic molecules interacting with the mineral deposition process, cellular processes, physiology, and other processes at the tissue and environmental levels are linked. Rather than being directed by a central control mechanism, biomineralization and embryogenesis can be viewed as an emergent behavior resulting from a complex system in which several sub-processes on very different temporal and spatial scales (ranging from nanometer and nanoseconds to meters and years) are connected into a multi-scale system. One of the few available options to understand such systems is by developing a multi-scale model of the system.
